0.title: Holy Exiles: Living the Gospel Under Pressure
0.overview:
The message. First Peter teaches Christians how to live as exiles. Three words in the greeting frame the whole letter: its readers are “elect exiles of the Dispersion” (1:1). They are chosen by God, and they are strangers and scattered in the world where they live. Both are true at once, and both must shape how they live. Peter does not explain why suffering comes; he shows how to endure it and what it means. His own summary at the end is that all of it, the suffering, the submission and the hope, is “the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (5:12).

Background: the writer. The letter names Peter as its author, “an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1), and he calls himself “a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ” (5:1). The man who once rebuked Jesus for speaking of the cross (Matthew 16:21–23), and then denied him, now returns again and again to the sufferings of Christ. The charge to “shepherd the flock of God” (5:2) echoes the commission the risen Lord gave him by the lake (John 21:15–17). He wrote “by Silvanus” (5:12), almost certainly the Silas who travelled with Paul, who probably helped with the writing, carried the letter, or both; and he sends greetings from Mark, “my son” (5:13). That Paul’s companions served Peter shows that the apostles were not rival parties.

Where and when. Peter writes from “Babylon” (5:13). Babylon was the city of Israel’s exile, and Jewish and Christian writers of the time used the name for Rome, as Revelation does: a fitting address for a letter about exile. Early Christian tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life and says he was put to death there under Nero, probably between AD 64 and 67. The letter was most likely written about AD 62–64, shortly before or at the start of Nero’s persecution, which followed the great fire of Rome in 64.

The first readers. They lived in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1:1), the Roman provinces of the north and centre of Asia Minor, now Turkey: a wide region of Black Sea ports, upland farms and scattered towns; the order of the names may trace a courier’s route through the churches. Some from Pontus, Cappadocia and Asia had heard Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). The readers were mainly converted Gentiles: 2:10 applies to them Hosea’s words about those who were “not a people”, and 4:3–4 recalls their old life of drinking parties and “lawless idolatry”, which their former friends could not understand them leaving. Yet Peter addresses them in the language of Israel: elect, exiles of the Dispersion, “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (2:9). The church now bears Israel’s name and calling, not by replacing Israel but as the one people of God in whom his promises are fulfilled.

What they faced. Their suffering was mostly the daily kind: being slandered “as evildoers” (2:12), shut out of the feasts and festivals that bound towns, trades and households together, held back in trade, mocked for bearing the new name “Christian” (4:16). Some were household slaves with harsh masters (2:18); some were wives of unbelieving husbands (3:1). A “fiery trial” (4:12) may have been coming. Peter treats all this not as strange but as the normal cost of belonging to God, shared by “your brotherhood throughout the world” (5:9).

Did Peter really write it? Many modern scholars think a later follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its polished Greek, unlikely from a Galilean fisherman, and to a setting of persecution they date later. But the letter claims Peter as author (1:1; 5:1), the early church received it without doubt, and the hostility it describes is that of neighbours, not a later empire-wide campaign. A fisherman from bilingual Galilee who had preached for thirty years could well write good Greek, especially with Silvanus at his side. The more likely conclusion is that Peter wrote it.

How the letter makes its case. The letter moves from who believers are, to how they live as exiles, to how they endure. Chapter 1 to 2:10 sets out their identity: born again “to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1:3), their faith tested as gold by fire, called to be holy as God is holy, ransomed by the precious blood of Christ, born of the word that remains when all flesh withers (chapter 1); then built as living stones into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, on Christ the rejected cornerstone (2:1–10). From 2:11 to 4:11 Peter shows how such exiles live among unbelievers: honourable conduct that silences slander; submission for the Lord’s sake to the emperor and governors, of slaves to masters even when unjust, and of wives to husbands, with husbands honouring their wives as fellow heirs (2:11–3:7); blessing in return for reviling and a gentle reason for their hope (3:8–17). All of this rests on Christ, who suffered once for sins and now reigns over every power (3:18–22), in a much-debated passage that this commentary reads, without dogmatism, as his proclamation of triumph over imprisoned spirits from Noah’s day. Then they are to arm themselves with his way of thinking, break with the old life, and love, show hospitality and use every gift as the end draws near (4:1–11). From 4:12 to the end Peter speaks directly to the fiery trial: rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings and entrust your souls to a faithful Creator (4:12–19); let the elders shepherd the flock and all clothe themselves with humility, cast their anxieties on God and resist the devil (5:1–11); then the greetings (5:12–14).

Where it leads: to Christ. The prophets, Peter says, searched to know when “the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” would come (1:11), and that order, suffering then glory, is the shape of the whole letter. Christ is the lamb without blemish (1:19), the stone rejected by men but chosen by God (2:4–8), the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53 who “himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (2:24), and the Chief Shepherd who will appear (5:4). In 2:21–25 and 3:18–22 his path becomes the pattern for his people: he suffered unjustly; he did not revile in return; he entrusted himself “to him who judges justly” (2:23); and God raised and vindicated him. Yet he is far more than an example. He died “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (3:18), and believers share his sufferings now so that they will share his glory (4:13). So Peter does not ask for gritted teeth; he gives certainty about how the story ends. The God who brought Jesus through the cross to the resurrection will bring his people through as well.

For us. First Peter speaks to every Christian who feels out of place: in a hostile workplace, an unbelieving home, a culture that finds faith strange or offensive. It tells you that you are not homeless but on the way home, with an inheritance that cannot fade. It calls you to answer slander with good deeds, insult with blessing, and questions with a gentle reason for your hope, and to cast all your anxieties on God, “because he cares for you” (5:7). And it promises that after you have suffered a little while, “the God of all grace … will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you” (5:10).

1.title: Living Hope: Election, Holiness, and the Imperishable Word
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 lays the letter’s foundation: before Peter says how exiles should live among their neighbours (2:11 onwards), he tells them who they are and what they have.

The message. You are chosen, born again and kept by God, with an inheritance no one can take from you; so your trials cannot be the last word, and your life should show that you belong to the God who bought you. Hope comes first, then holiness: every command rests on something God has already done.

Why it was said. The readers, mostly Gentile converts, had become outsiders in their own towns, slandered and shut out of the old feasts (see the introduction). It would have been easy to read their troubles as a sign that God had left them, or to slip back into the old ways.

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting names them “elect exiles” and shows Father, Spirit and Son at work in their choosing (vv. 1–2). The thanksgiving shows what they have: a living hope and a kept inheritance (vv. 3–5), trials that prove faith as fire proves gold (vv. 6–7), joy in a Christ they have not seen (vv. 8–9), and a salvation prophets searched for and angels long to see (vv. 10–12). Then the commands: hope fully (v. 13); be holy as God is holy (vv. 14–16); live in reverent fear before the Father who judges, knowing the price of your ransom (vv. 17–21); and love one another earnestly as brothers born of the imperishable word that outlasts all flesh (vv. 22–25). Throughout, Peter sets the imperishable against the perishable: the inheritance (v. 4), the ransom (vv. 18–19), the seed of new birth (v. 23).

Where it leads. The chapter rests on Christ. His resurrection is the ground of the hope (vv. 3, 21); his revelation is the day everything comes into view (vv. 7, 13); his blood, the blood of a spotless lamb foreknown before the foundation of the world, is the price of their freedom (vv. 19–20). The prophets foretold “the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (v. 11) without seeing how they fitted; Peter had seen both, and tells exiles that their road has the same shape.

For us. Whenever following Christ leaves you out of place, this chapter tells you to read it as the feeling of an exile, not of a reject. Begin where Peter begins, by blessing God, and let hope, holiness and love grow from there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chosen by God and strangers in the world: both are true of believers at once, and the second is no evidence against the first. Peter names his readers with two words that do not normally belong together, elect and exiles (v. 1), and then shows the whole Trinity behind their choosing: the Father’s foreknowledge, the Spirit’s setting apart, and the Son’s blood, which makes them a covenant people as Israel was made one at Sinai (v. 2). To people treated as outsiders, it says that being out of place is what belonging to God looks like in a world that is not yet home.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elect Exiles

Chosen by God and strangers in the world, both at once, and the second is no evidence against the first. Father, Spirit and Son are all at work in their salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scattered believers across five provinces were being slandered and excluded.

Now: Being out of place in the world is no sign that God has forgotten you.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chosen by God and strangers in the world: both are true of these believers, and the first explains the second. Behind their choosing stands the whole Trinity: the Father chose them, the Spirit set them apart, and the Son’s blood made them his covenant people.

Peter, an apostle. Simon was his name; Jesus gave him another, Petros, rock (in Aramaic, Cephas) (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). He does not call himself chief apostle, the rock on which the church is built, or first bishop of Rome, and later calls himself simply a fellow elder (5:1). He led the twelve and preached at Pentecost (Acts 2), but an apostle is one sent, and everything depends on the sender.

Who is writing. This is the man who swore three times that he did not know Christ, and to whom the Lord had said, “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). This letter is Peter doing what he was told. He knows from the inside how faith can buckle under social pressure, and how Christ holds on to it anyway, and he tells people under social pressure that this is “the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (5:12).

Elect exiles. Two words that do not normally belong together; the whole letter lives in the tension between them. Elect (eklektois): chosen, God’s own, the language of Israel. Exiles (parepidēmois): resident foreigners with no standing where they live, the word used of the patriarchs, who “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). Peter puts the highest status beside the lowest and says: both, at once. Treated as outsiders, they might naturally conclude that God had forgotten them; Peter rules that out in his first sentence. Being outsiders is what being loved by God looks like in a world that is not yet their home, for “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). The more you belong to God, the less you will fully belong anywhere else, and that is not failure but a sign of whose you are (John 15:19).

Of the Dispersion. Scattering (diaspora, as in James 1:1) was the name for the Jews scattered among the nations. Peter lays it over a church made mostly of Gentiles, whose grandparents had worshipped Zeus (see the introduction): they now belong to the scattered people of God, waiting to be gathered into the inheritance kept in heaven (v. 4). Israel’s story has become their story.

Foreknowledge. Verse 2 shows the whole Trinity in one salvation: the Father’s foreknowledge is where it begins, the Spirit’s sanctifying how it reaches us, obedience to Christ and sprinkling with his blood what it is for. Foreknowledge (prognōsis) is not God peering forward to see who would choose him. In Scripture, to know someone is to set your regard on them: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth”, God tells Israel (Amos 3:2), and he was not admitting he had no information about Egypt. Foreknowledge is love fixed beforehand, not information gathered in advance (Romans 8:29; 11:2). Peter uses the word of Christ in verse 20 (chosen and appointed), and at Pentecost of the cross: “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23).

In the sanctification of the Spirit. Sanctification (hagiasmos) is being set apart. The Father’s choice in eternity reaches a particular life, in a particular town, on a particular day, as the Spirit takes hold of a person for God and brings him to faith (2 Thessalonians 2:13). A pagan in Cappadocia may have thought he was simply listening to a travelling preacher. The Spirit was marking him out as God’s own.

Obedience and sprinkling. This reaches back to Sinai. Moses read the Book of the Covenant, the people answered, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient”, and Moses threw the blood on them: “Behold the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:3–8; Hebrews 9:19–20). Obedience and blood, in that order: that was the moment Israel became God’s nation. Peter tells scattered foreigners that the same thing has happened to them, under a better covenant with better blood.

The better blood. Peter had heard that covenant made. In the upper room Jesus took the cup and said, “this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). Moses threw the blood of bulls; the Son of God shed his own. The blood that made Peter’s readers God’s people was not splashed on them from an altar; it ran from the veins of the Lord who loved them. So election ends not in a privilege to admire but in a people who obey Christ and are cleansed by him, and keep being cleansed, for the sprinkling is also the ongoing provision for people who still fail (1 John 1:7).

Multiplied. Not merely given: Peter writes to people whose troubles were multiplying, and prays that grace would multiply faster. Grace comes before peace, because peace is what grace produces.

Before Rome had an emperor. Before Rome had an emperor or the world had a sun, the Father had set his love on a handful of people who would one day meet in a back room in Asia Minor and be laughed at by their neighbours. The Spirit went and found them, one by one. The Son poured out the blood that would make them his. The God who scattered them will gather them, every one, into a home that cannot be taken away.

What it does not mean. Being exiles does not mean being indifferent to the place where they live. They are to do good there and honour its authorities (2:12–17), seeking the welfare of the city (Jeremiah 29:7), while holding everything here with an open hand.

In everyday life. The next time you feel out of place, at work, in your family, in a conversation where everyone laughs at what you cannot laugh at, name it: the feeling of an exile, not of a reject. Then say the other word over yourself: chosen.

Does election mean God does not want everyone to be saved? It means salvation begins with God, which is why anyone is saved at all. The gospel is preached to everyone, and everyone who comes to Christ is welcomed (John 6:37). No one will ever be turned away who wanted Christ and was refused because he was not chosen; the doctrine works the other way. It tells the believer that his coming was God’s doing, and that the God who began it will finish it. Election is written to comfort believers, not as a riddle for outsiders, and its first effect in this letter is to steady people who felt rejected by everyone.

How can I know I am one of the elect? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, but by looking at what election produces in time, named in this very verse: the Spirit setting you apart, obedience to Jesus Christ, the sprinkling of his blood. Are you trusting Christ’s blood, and nothing else, for your cleansing? Do you want to obey him, and grieve when you do not? Then you are looking at the fingerprints of the Father’s choice. Peter later tells his readers to make their calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:10), not by speculation but by a growing life of faith and love.

Where Christians differ: is election based on foreseen faith? Arminian Christians read “according to the foreknowledge of God” that way, out of a real wish to guard human responsibility. This commentary’s view: God’s foreknowledge here is his loving choice beforehand, as Christ was foreknown (1:20), and faith is the result of election, not its cause (Acts 13:48).

Uncertain wording. The Greek is compressed: literally, for obedience and sprinkling of blood of Jesus Christ. “Of Jesus Christ” plainly goes with the blood; whether it also names the one obeyed is less certain. Most translations, like the ESV, take it as obedience to Christ, which fits the echo of Exodus 24. Some read obedience on its own, to the gospel (compare “obedience to the truth”, v. 22). On either reading the cleansing comes from Christ’s blood.
verseByVerse.note: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia were Roman provinces covering much of modern Turkey. Peter probably wrote from Rome in the early 60s AD, shortly before Nero’s persecution. The readers were mostly Gentile believers, now “exiles” in their own society.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–12 — Born Again to a Living Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has given his people a new birth into a hope that cannot die, so they can rejoice even while they grieve. Peter blesses God for the new birth, the living hope grounded in Christ’s resurrection, and an inheritance kept for them while they are kept for it (vv. 3–5). Trials are therefore not a contradiction but a refining fire that proves faith genuine (vv. 6–7), and they love and rejoice in a Christ they have not seen (vv. 8–9). What they have is no small thing: prophets searched for it, and angels long to look into it (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Kept, and Keeping

Born again to a living hope, believers have an inheritance kept in heaven and are themselves guarded by God's power until it is revealed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prophets searched their own words about Christ’s sufferings and the glories to follow.

Now: Trials test faith as fire tests gold, and faith is worth far more.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his great mercy God has given his people new life, a hope that cannot die and an inheritance that cannot be lost, and he keeps the inheritance for them and them for it.

Blessed be the God. Peter opens with praise, not instruction, and in Greek the sentence has no verb: it is a cry, not a statement. Blessed (eulogētos): worthy of praise. It is the opening of Ephesians 1:3 and 2 Corinthians 1:3, the shape of the blessings a devout Jew said many times a day, now filled with new content: God is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Peter does not begin with his readers’ problems but with God, because problems look different once God has been seen.

According to his great mercy. Not according to their goodness, potential or need. Mercy is kindness to those who deserve the opposite, and Peter knew how much mercy it had taken to make a Christian of him.

He has caused us to be born again. To beget again (anagennaō): only Peter uses the verb (here and v. 23), but the idea goes back to Jesus’ words to Nicodemus (John 3:3–8; compare James 1:18). The grammar is the point: he caused us. Nobody arranges his own birth, the second any more than the first. A Christian is not someone who turned over a new leaf but someone to whom God gave a new life, and you can see the difference. Before, the things of God left him cold, as a dead man is cold to music; now he finds himself wanting God, trusting Christ and hating his own sin, and that new wanting is the life God has put in him (Ezekiel 36:26; Ephesians 2:4–5).

To a living hope. Not a lively feeling but a hope that is alive. Most of what the world calls hope is a wish with its fingers crossed. Christian hope is a certainty not yet seen, alive because it rests on a living Saviour.

Through the resurrection. The hope rests on an event. A dead man’s promises expire with him; these do not, and no one knew it better than Peter. On the Saturday after the crucifixion his hope was as dead as the body in the tomb: the man he believed was the Messiah had been executed, and he himself had denied him. Then on Sunday he ran to the tomb and found it empty, and that day the Lord appeared to Simon himself (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5). When Peter writes of a living hope through the resurrection, he is describing his own Easter. His hope was dead, and it was raised with Christ.

Imperishable, undefiled, and unfading. The inheritance (klēronomia) is described by three Greek words that each begin with the letter meaning “not”. Imperishable (aphtharton): it cannot decay. Undefiled (amianton): sin cannot pollute it. Unfading (amaranton): it cannot wither like a flower (the amaranth was named for this). Israel’s land could be invaded, defiled and lost, and had been; death, sin and time take everything we own. This inheritance is beyond the reach of all three. Some of Peter’s readers may well have lost property, or been cut out of a family will, for becoming Christians. He tells them what they have not lost.

What is the inheritance? Not a mansion with a number on the door, but God himself and everything he gives with himself: the new heavens and new earth, a resurrection body, the sight of Christ, sinless fellowship with all his people, and the end of every tear (Romans 8:17; Revelation 21:3–4). It is not earned as wages but received as children, because an inheritance comes by birth, which is why Peter puts the new birth and the inheritance in one sentence.

Kept in heaven for you. Reserved in the past and still reserved now: that is the force of the Greek tense. No thief, no inflation, no confiscating magistrate in Bithynia can touch it.

Guarded through faith. Guarded (phrouroumenous) is a military word, for soldiers posted around a city, and the tense is present: the guarding goes on now. So the inheritance is kept for you, and you are kept for it, by the hands that hold the stars. By God’s power: the guarding is his work. Through faith: the means he uses. He keeps us by keeping us believing.

Ready to be revealed. Salvation is not still being assembled in heaven. It is complete, and waiting to be unveiled at Christ’s return.

What it does not mean. Not that believers can be careless: a person who shrugs at Christ and says he is safe anyway has misread the promise. But for the one who wants Christ, God himself guarantees that the believing will go on.

In everyday life. List what you are afraid of losing: health, a job, someone you love, your own mind in old age. Beside it write “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading”, to put the first list in its place. Then pray in Peter’s order: first blessing, then the request. It is very hard to panic and bless at the same time.

Does “through faith” mean my security depends on my holding on? Faith is the means by which God guards us, not a condition that hands our safety back to us; the faith itself is his gift, kept by his power. Think of a father holding a small child’s hand on a busy road. The child holds on too, but he is not safe because of his grip. He is safe because his father’s hand is round his.

What about people who seemed to believe and then walked away? Scripture is honest that some do, and explains them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19; Matthew 13:20–21). Not everyone who joins a church has been born again, and seed on rocky ground can spring up and wither. That is sobering, but not a threat to the anxious believer: the one who fears falling away and runs to Christ is showing the very faith by which God guards him. If someone you love has drifted, do not conclude too quickly either way. Pray, keep the door open, and remember that some who wander are sheep who will be brought back.

Where Christians differ: can a believer lose this inheritance? Some traditions teach that a true believer can fall away finally and be lost. This commentary’s view: Peter teaches a double security: the inheritance is kept in heaven for us, and we are guarded by God’s power through faith for it. Neither can fail. This is the perseverance of the saints: those whom God has begotten again he will keep to the end, not apart from their faith but through it, which he himself sustains (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; Jude 24).

verseByVerse.quote: In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers can rejoice while they grieve, because their trials are brief, purposeful and refining a faith worth more than gold, which Christ will honour when he appears.

In this you rejoice. In what has just been described: the new birth, the living hope, the kept inheritance. The joy rests on something outside their circumstances, which is the only way it can survive the trials named next. Rejoice is a strong word, exult (Luke 1:47), and it is present: not when this is over, but now.

For a little while, if necessary. Three phrases limit the trials, and each is a mercy. “Now”: they are temporary. “For a little while”: short beside the imperishable inheritance (2 Corinthians 4:17). And “if necessary”, the tender one: they are not random but come only when God sees a need. “Various” trials are literally many-coloured (James 1:2), the word Peter uses for God’s “varied grace” (4:10). The trials come in many colours, and so does the grace.

You have been grieved. The word is used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37). Peter does not pretend joy cancels pain: “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). A Christian at a graveside is allowed to weep. He is given not the absence of grief but a joy beneath it that grief cannot reach.

Tested genuineness. The word (dokimion) belongs to the assayer who tests metal: the proven part left when the fire has taken the rest. The refiner, as the old picture is told, kept going until he could see his own face in the molten metal. Trials are meant not to destroy faith but to prove and purify it, and the refiner is never careless with the heat (Malachi 3:3).

More precious than gold. The comparison is exact. Gold is refined by fire and still perishes; faith is refined the same way and does not. Same process, more precious product: that is Peter’s answer to a suffering congregation asking what all this is for. If men put gold through the furnace, will God not do as much for faith? Job found it out in the dark: “when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold” (Job 23:10; Zechariah 13:9).

At the revelation of Jesus Christ. The praise lands at the revelation (apokalypsis), the unveiling of Christ at his return, not now. On a set day believers will be shown to have been right, which makes “for a little while” a real comfort. Whose praise? Christ’s praise of the believer, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21), and all of it to God’s glory. The Lord who is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11) will stand before the universe and acknowledge the faith of a slave girl in Pontus who would not deny him.

The Refiner went into the fire first. The Refiner sits by the furnace and does not leave. He went into the fire himself first, on a hill outside Jerusalem, where the heat was not measured and did not stop until it was finished, so that the fire his people pass through would only ever refine them and never consume them.

In everyday life. Name your trial, and say Peter’s three things to God about it: it is for a little while; it is not random; it is producing something more precious than gold. Then ask him what impurity he is burning away, and to keep his hand on the fire.

Is God the one sending my suffering? Scripture holds two things together. God is sovereign over every trial, so nothing reaches his child by accident; that is what “if necessary” means. And he is never the author of evil: much suffering comes through the sin of others, a fallen world, or the devil (5:8). Joseph’s brothers meant evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), both true of one event. You need not decide whether a trial came from God’s hand or someone’s malice; only that it cannot leave God’s hand, and that he intends it for your good.

How do I know if my faith is genuine? The fire shows it: not whether you feel strong, but whether under pressure you still turn towards Christ. Genuine faith may be shaken and weak, as Peter’s was, but it keeps coming back to the same place: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). Faith that was really faith in comfort leaves when the comfort goes. If your trial has driven you to pray more and lean harder on Christ, the test is already showing your faith to be real.

Uncertain wording. “In this” could point back to all of verses 3–5, or only to “the last time” in verse 5 (in which you will rejoice); and “you rejoice” could be a statement, a command, or a present with future sense. Most take it as the ESV does, a statement about present joy resting on verses 3–5, which fits verse 8, where the joy is plainly present.

verseByVerse.quote: Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory, obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers love and trust a Christ they have never seen, and already taste the joy of the salvation he will complete.

Though you have not seen him. Remember who is writing. Peter had seen him: pulled in nets with him, walked on water towards him, watched him transfigured, and denied him while “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). Of all who could have written this sentence, he is the one for whom it is not true. Yet there is no hint of superiority in it. He honours their position, and the Lord had already said where the greater blessing lay: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29).

You love him. Peter puts love before faith, and perhaps he could not help it. Beside a charcoal fire the risen Lord had asked him three times, “do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). Now he tells Gentiles who were never on that beach that they love him too. The question marks every Christian: not merely whether we agree with him, but whether we love him.

Inexpressible and filled with glory. Peter has no words for their joy. “Filled with glory” most likely means the glory of the age to come has already begun to seep into it: a foretaste, arriving in hard lives, and not dependent on circumstances, because it does not come from them.

The outcome of your faith. Obtaining is a word for carrying off a prize, and it is present: you are obtaining it now, while the grief of verse 6 goes on. “Souls” means the whole person; this salvation includes the resurrection.

You do not now see him. He is the one whom angels see face to face, and he has chosen to be loved, for now, by people who have never seen him. He hides himself in a word and a Spirit, and somehow, from a back street in Cappadocia to a hospital bed tonight, he wins hearts that have never looked into his eyes. But the not-seeing has a time limit: “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

How can I love someone I have never seen? As you can love a person through letters before you meet, only more so, because Christ is not absent: he speaks in his word, is present by his Spirit, and shows you who he is in the Gospels. Love for Christ is not mainly a feeling you work up. It grows as you look at him, and shows itself in wanting to please him, trusting him, missing him and longing to see him (John 14:21). If you are drawn to him, grieved when you dishonour him and glad when he is honoured, you love him, even if the feeling is quiet.

What if I do not feel this joy at all? Then you are in the company of many saints, and of psalmists who wrote whole songs from the dark (Psalm 88). Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, not a test you pass or fail each morning. It can be buried under depression, grief, exhaustion or illness, and none of those means Christ has left you; if low mood lingers, talk with your pastor or a biblical counsellor and see your doctor, for the body affects the soul. Keep looking at Christ, keep using the means of grace, and tell God honestly that you want to rejoice in him and cannot. Peter’s joy rests on facts, not feelings: you are loved, kept and being saved. The feeling will come back; the facts never left.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The salvation these believers have is the one the prophets foretold without fully understanding it, and that angels long to look into. Peter tells a harassed congregation of foreigners, raised on Homer, that Isaiah, Jeremiah and Daniel were speaking of grace that was to be theirs.

Searched and inquired carefully. Two strong verbs: investigated diligently, like miners tunnelling for ore. The prophets were not dictation machines but puzzled readers of what they had written, as Daniel studied Jeremiah and asked about his own visions (Daniel 9:2; 12:8–9).

The Spirit of Christ in them. The prophets carried the Spirit of a Christ not yet born (Romans 8:9), which can only mean he existed before Bethlehem. Prophecy was not their own invention (2 Peter 1:21).

The sufferings and the glories. Predicted (promartyromenon): testified beforehand. Peter names what the prophets could not work out. A suffering figure (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22) and a glorified one (Psalm 110; Daniel 7) were both in the text, and no one could see how they fitted. Two Messiahs, or one who would suffer and then be glorified? Nobody could tell until it happened. Then the risen Christ asked, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:25–27, 44–46), and Peter was in the room that evening when he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. Note “glories”, plural: resurrection, ascension, reign and return. And the pattern is his readers’ too: suffering first, then glory (4:13; 5:10).

Not themselves but you. They were told, in effect, that the answer was not for their generation, and they went on writing. Isaiah wrote of the Servant “pierced for our transgressions” seven centuries before anyone saw it. Anyone labouring for fruit he will not live to see is in good company: the Sunday school teacher who never learns what became of the children, the missionary translating a Bible he will not see printed, the mother praying for grandchildren not yet born. The prophets served people they would never meet, and Peter tells his readers that they were those people.

The Holy Spirit sent from heaven. The Spirit who spoke through the prophets spoke through the preachers who brought the gospel to Asia Minor. This is Pentecost (Acts 2), and Peter had stood in the middle of it. The unnamed preacher who came to Pontus was finishing a sentence Isaiah had begun.

Angels long to look. Long (epithymousin): eagerly desire. Look (parakypsai): stoop down and peer in, the word used of the disciples bending to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5, 11) and of looking into the perfect law (James 1:25). Peter himself had stooped and looked into that tomb (Luke 24:12). He pictures angels leaning over the edge of heaven, trying to see. They have never needed redeeming, and it fascinates them. Through the church God’s manifold wisdom is made known to the heavenly powers (Ephesians 3:10), and there is joy before the angels over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10). What angels long to see, believers possess.

Every line ran towards one hill. For a thousand years the Spirit of Christ spoke of him through men who could not see his face: Moses in a lamb, David in a forsaken sufferer, Isaiah in a crushed Servant, Daniel in a Son of Man on the clouds. All the lines of all the prophets ran towards one hill and one empty tomb, and what prophets searched for and angels stoop to see is ours.

In everyday life. If the gospel has become familiar, read Isaiah 53 slowly today, remembering that the man who wrote it did not know the name of the one he described, and longed to. Ask God to give you back some of the wonder.

So should I look for Christ in every verse of the Old Testament? Look for him in its whole story rather than under every stone. Every part of the Old Testament is heading somewhere: the sacrifices show what sin costs, the kings what a true king must be, the prophets judgment and a coming rescue, and the psalms give the very words Christ would pray. Ask of each passage what it shows about God, about sin and the need for a Saviour, and how Christ fulfils it. He said of the Scriptures, “it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39).

Why do angels not experience salvation? No Saviour came for fallen angels. Christ took human nature, not angelic (Hebrews 2:16), and died for human sinners. The loyal angels never needed saving, and the rebels have not been offered it. So they watch with wonder something done for a race lower than themselves, and see depths of God’s love and wisdom they would not otherwise know. The gospel you heard as an ordinary Sunday sermon is something the highest creatures in the universe study.

Uncertain wording. “What person or time” (tina ē poion kairon) can also be read what time or what kind of time. On that reading the prophets asked only when, and in what circumstances, the Messiah would come; on the ESV’s they also asked who he would be. Both are possible Greek, and the difference is small.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — Be Holy, for I Am Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because of this salvation, live as people who belong to God: hopeful, holy, reverent and loving. Each command rests on something God has done. Set your hope fully on the grace still coming (v. 13). Be holy, because the God who called you is holy (vv. 14–16). Live in reverent fear, because your Father is also the impartial Judge, and your ransom cost the precious blood of Christ, the Lamb foreknown before the world began (vv. 17–21). Love one another earnestly, because you were born again into one family by the imperishable word of God, which outlasts all flesh (vv. 22–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of a Child

Be holy, because the one who called you is holy. Call on him as Father who judges impartially, and remember the price of your ransom: the precious blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had been ransomed from empty ways handed down from their ancestors.

Now: All flesh withers, but the word of the Lord remains, and that word is the gospel preached to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of this salvation, believers are to gather their minds, stay clear-headed and fix their hope wholly on the grace Christ will bring when he returns. The first command in the letter is a command to hope, because holiness, love and endurance all grow out of it: a person who knows what is waiting for him can bear a great deal on the road.

Therefore, preparing your minds for action. Peter never gives a command without a reason. The phrase is literally girding up the loins of your mind. A man in a long robe tucked it into his belt before he could run or work, or he would trip. So gather up scattered, wandering thoughts: not more feeling but a mind pulled together and ready, which the Spirit who set them apart (v. 2) helps them do. There is a memory of the Passover, eaten with belts fastened, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11; Luke 12:35). A Christian’s mind is to be packed for a journey.

Being sober-minded. The opposite of drunk: clear-headed, seeing things as they are (4:7; 5:8). A person can be drunk on the world’s pleasures, its panic or its endless news, and the effect is the same: he cannot see straight.

Set your hope fully. Without reserve, with nothing held back for a second option. Peter does not promise the trials will stop; he tells them where to put their hope so that it is not destroyed if they do not.

The grace that will be brought to you. Like a ship already on the horizon, that grace set out from heaven when the Son left the Father’s side. It was paid for at the cross, guaranteed at the empty tomb, and comes nearer every day, with nothing in the universe able to stop it. When he appears he will not come empty-handed: he will bring everything he has kept for us, and himself above all.

In everyday life. Watch what you reach for when you feel low: the phone, the fridge, the news. At that moment tuck the robe in, and say one sentence to yourself about what is coming at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

How do I actually set my hope on something? Hope is a direction you give your mind, not only a feeling: think about what is coming, again and again, until it shapes your expectations. Read what Scripture says about Christ’s return and the new creation (Revelation 21–22; 1 Corinthians 15). When you catch yourself resting your security on something else, a promotion, a relationship, a medical result, name it and turn back: that would be good, but it is not my hope. Sing about heaven; talk about it with other Christians. Hope that is never fed shrinks; hope that is fed carries you.

Is hoping in heaven not just escapism? It is the opposite. Whatever we hope in will rule us: if my hope is a career, a marriage or a comfortable retirement, I will be crushed when it fails, or tempted to do almost anything to keep it. A person whose hope is fixed on Christ’s return can afford to lose those things, and so can afford to be honest, generous and brave now. Peter’s readers were to do good among their neighbours (2:12), not retreat from them. The people with the surest future have usually been the most useful in the present.

Uncertain wording. “Fully” (teleiōs) stands between “being sober-minded” and “set your hope”, and could belong with either: be fully sober, or hope fully. Most translations, like the ESV, take it with hope, the main command. Either way Peter asks for a mind wholly clear and a hope wholly set.

verseByVerse.quote: As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s children must no longer be shaped by the cravings of their old life, but be holy in all of life, because the God who called them is holy.

As obedient children. Literally “children of obedience”, a Hebrew way of saying that obedience is what they are made of. Born again into God’s family (v. 3), they hear not a sergeant’s rule but the family likeness a father expects to see growing in his children.

Do not be conformed. Pressed into a mould, as in Romans 12:2. The pressure is constant and unnoticed: a jelly does not decide to take the shape of the mould; it simply sits there long enough. Passions are the cravings that ran the old life. “Your former ignorance” is a merciful description of a Gentile past, not only wickedness but not-knowing. Peter does not excuse the old life, but he refuses to define them by it: that is who you were, not who you are, and what you now know leaves no excuse for going back.

As he who called you is holy. God called them with an effectual call, not merely an invitation but the inward summons that actually brings a person to faith (2:9, 21; 5:10). Then the startling standard: not an improvement on the culture, nor the best human example, nor the average Christian in your church, but God himself. Holy (hagios) means set apart, other, of a different order: utterly pure and morally perfect. The seraphim cry it three times, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), and cover their faces.

In all your conduct. Holiness in conduct is a life that visibly belongs to God and not to the world around it, and “all” closes the loophole: work, home, speech, money, the browser history, the tax return, the thoughts nobody else hears.

Since it is written. The quotation is from Leviticus 11:44–45, repeated there (19:2; 20:7, 26). Peter does something bold: a command given to Israel at Sinai he applies without adjustment to Gentile converts in Bithynia, because they are now the covenant people, as he will argue in chapter 2. And the reason is a person, not a rule: “for I am holy”. Holiness is no optional extra for keen Christians. It reflects the God who called us, and without it “no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14).

The Holy One in a fishing boat. Peter had met holiness at close range. After the great catch he fell at Jesus’ knees: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8), Isaiah’s “Woe is me” in a fishing boat. Later he confessed, “you are the Holy One of God” (John 6:69; the KJV, following later manuscripts, reads the Christ, the Son of the living God). And the glory Isaiah saw when the seraphim cried holy was the glory of Christ (John 12:41). So the holiness of Leviticus is not an abstract standard. It walked the shore of Galilee, touched lepers without being defiled, and committed no sin (2:22). And the Holy One did not depart from the sinful man; he called him, and calls us, to be made like himself. None of us keeps this command perfectly (1 John 1:8). He kept it in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so our stumbling holiness is accepted for his sake while his Spirit makes it real.

What it does not mean. Not that we become holy in order to be accepted: we are called and accepted by grace, and holiness is the response. Nor that holiness means withdrawing from the world; it means being different within it.

Where do I start? Where the pressure to conform is strongest for you: for one person the tongue at work, for another entertainment, money, or anger at home. Ask: in this one area, what would I do if I were really from somewhere else? Then do it, relying on the Spirit and not on willpower alone, and confess quickly when you fail. Holiness grows like a garden, not like a light switched on, and it grows best in people who are not afraid to tell God the truth.

Is it possible to be holy as God is holy? In one sense believers already are: set apart as God’s own people (2:9). In another it is a lifelong work, real growth by the Spirit’s power, never complete in this life (1 John 1:8). God supplies what he commands; the standard is himself, and the goal is likeness to Christ at his appearing.

Does holiness mean being serious and joyless? No. The holiest man who ever lived was called a glutton and a drunkard because he ate and drank freely, and with sinners (Matthew 11:19). Holiness is wholeness, a life with nothing rotten in it, and it removes what spoils joy: guilt, secrecy, slavery to appetite. Holy people laugh freely because they have nothing to hide. What it excludes is the cheap laughter that depends on cruelty or filth (Ephesians 5:4), and the joy that needs sin to be fun.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one's deeds, conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers call God Father, but he is also the Judge who weighs every life without favouritism, so they are to live in reverent fear for the whole time of their exile.

If you call on him as Father. “If” does not express doubt; it means since you do. People who had prayed to statues of Artemis now call the living God Father (Matthew 6:9).

Who judges impartially. In the same breath, the Judge. Impartially is literally without receiving the face (James 2:1): God is not swayed by position or connection, which is terrifying to the advantaged and good news to people at the bottom of every social ladder. Having him as Father does not exempt us from his evaluation of our deeds (2 Corinthians 5:10); it means the one evaluating them loves us.

Conduct yourselves with fear. “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), and Peter does not contradict it. This is not terror of condemnation, for he has just called God Father, but the reverence of a child who loves his father and does not want to displease him (Proverbs 9:10). The wrong fear hides in the garden like Adam. The right fear comes near, takes its shoes off like Moses, and listens.

Throughout the time of your exile. The exile word again, now with a duration: it has a beginning and an end (2:11). A man who truly fears God has little capacity left for fearing anybody else. The neighbours could slander them, but the opinion that finally mattered was their Father’s.

The Judge we have met. Peter learned this in a Roman officer’s house: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality”, he told Cornelius, and in the same sermon announced that Jesus “is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10:34, 42; John 5:22). So the impartial Judge has a face of his own: the face of the one who was judged in our place, before a partial high priest and a cowardly governor. Never fooled by a face, he has adopted the guilty at the cost of his Son, so the courtroom where every work will be weighed is presided over by the one who loves us most. We may call God Father only because the Son taught us to and died to make it true.

In everyday life. When you pray “Our Father in heaven”, pause on both parts: Father, so you can come close; in heaven, so you come with reverence.

If God judges according to deeds, does that contradict justification by faith alone? No. Justification is the Judge’s own verdict that we are righteous, given not for anything in us but because Christ’s obedience and death are counted to us (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The faith that justifies shows itself in deeds, and at the judgment those deeds are its evidence (Romans 2:6–7). Our standing rests on Christ; our deeds show that we belong to him, and are rewarded by grace.

How does fearing God free me from fearing people? Fear always looks to whoever holds the final verdict. If colleagues, family or social media hold it, I will bend to them. If God holds it, their verdicts shrink to their real size: real, sometimes painful, but not final. “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). Before a hard conversation, ask: what will my Father think of this, and does anything else finally matter? That question has made timid people brave for two thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers were set free from the empty way of life handed down to them at the highest price ever paid: the blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb. Reverence rests on knowing what was paid.

Ransomed. A word from the slave market, a price paid to secure a release (Mark 10:45), with the exodus behind it, when Israel was redeemed by the blood of the Passover lamb.

The futile ways inherited from your forefathers. A striking thing to tell Gentiles, for it names what most of them would have called their heritage. Futile (mataias), empty, achieving nothing, is the standard biblical verdict on idols. Inherited (patroparadotou), handed down by your fathers, is the sharp word: these ways came down to them; they did not choose them. Nobody escapes what a family has always taken for granted just by deciding to; that is why a ransom was needed, not advice. Christ’s blood frees us from empty traditions and cultural patterns, as well as from guilt.

The modern inheritance. We have our own: anger, drinking, coldness or quiet despair running through three generations, and assumptions absorbed before we could read, that you are what you earn and death is the end. Many a Christian has been the first in a long family line to be bought out of the old ways.

Not with silver or gold. The two most durable currencies of the ancient world, and Peter calls them perishable. All the gold in Rome could not have paid for one lie.

The precious blood of Christ. Precious (timios): costly, honoured. Christ’s blood is of infinite worth because he is the infinite Son of God; Paul speaks of “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). You can tell what something is worth to its buyer by what he paid for it. That is the comfort for people treated as worthless: their value is set by what Christ spent on them, not by what their neighbours, or they themselves, thought them worth. “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

A lamb without blemish or spot. Without blemish (amōmos): no defect. Without spot (aspilos): no stain. The Passover lamb had to be inspected and found flawless (Exodus 12:5), as did every sacrifice (Leviticus 22:19–25). Peter, whose brother Andrew heard John the Baptist say, “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John 1:29, 36–40), applies the inspection language to Christ. Pilate and Herod found no guilt in him (Luke 23:14–15), the false witnesses could not agree (Mark 14:56), and the ruler of this world had no claim on him (John 14:30). He was led like a lamb to the slaughter and opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Only a spotless life could be offered in place of stained ones (Revelation 5:6–12).

Bought out of the market. Christ walked into the market where we were being sold and paid for us with himself. The futile ways of our fathers end at his cross, and a new family history begins there.

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to Satan, who has no rightful claim over us. The price satisfied God’s justice (Romans 3:24–26), and it frees us from the futile ways of verse 18.

Why did it have to be blood? Because sin deserves death, and “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Hebrews 9:22). Blood stands for a life given up in death. God could not simply overlook sin and remain just; the penalty had to be paid, and in love he paid it himself, in his Son, who “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (2:24). This is penal substitution: Christ took the punishment we deserved, so that we go free. The blood is not a magical substance; it is the sign of a death, and that death was ours.

verseByVerse.quote: He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s coming to die was God’s plan before creation, carried out in these last times for believers’ sake, and because God raised him, their faith and hope can rest on God.

Foreknown before the foundation of the world. The same word as of the readers in verse 2: not merely foreseen, but chosen and appointed. The cross was no plan B, improvised after things went wrong; the Lamb was in view before Genesis 1 (Ephesians 1:4; Acts 2:23).

Made manifest in the last times. Made manifest (phanerōthentos): made visible. This is the incarnation, God’s hidden purpose stepping into history on a particular day. “The last times” is the New Testament’s name for the period the readers are in (Hebrews 1:2): the final era began at Bethlehem, and we are living in it, not waiting for it. So God has nothing left to add to the work of salvation; the decisive acts are done, and the next great event on his calendar is Christ’s return (Hebrews 9:26–28).

For the sake of you. The eternal purpose was made manifest for a scattered group of slandered foreigners in Pontus and Bithynia. It had you in view too, not as a statistic, but as one for whom the Son came.

Through him are believers in God. Christ is not only the one we believe in, but the one through whom we come to believe in God at all (John 14:6).

Raised him and gave him glory. The world said no to Jesus, and God said yes (Acts 2:32–36; Philippians 2:9). Then the logic: “so that your faith and hope are in God”. Peter points to the resurrection here not mainly to prove that it happened, but to show whom we can trust, the argument of verse 3 made a second time. A God who raises the dead can be trusted with an inheritance.

If God planned the cross, were those who crucified Jesus guilty? Yes. Scripture holds both together without embarrassment. At Pentecost Peter said that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same sentence, “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). God ordained the event for our salvation; Judas, Caiaphas and Pilate did it for wicked reasons and were answerable for it. God’s sovereignty never makes human choices unreal. It means that even the worst thing men ever did was taken up into the best thing God ever did.

verseByVerse.quote: Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth for a sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel has already purified believers for genuine love of one another, so they are to love each other earnestly and from the heart.

Having purified your souls. Something already done, as the Greek tense shows: at conversion, through obedience to the truth, the gospel believed and acted on (Acts 15:9).

For a sincere brotherly love. The purifying had an aim, and the aim was other people. Brotherly love is family affection. Sincere is literally not play-acted, the Greek word for an actor with “not” in front of it: love can be put on as a performance, and Peter rules that out. “From a pure heart” says the same from the inside: undivided motives, not loving in order to be thought loving. You have been purified for love; therefore love. The command is needed because what is true of us is not yet automatic in us.

Earnestly. Ektenōs: fervently, without letting up, from a root meaning to stretch out; love kept at full stretch. Peter had reason to know the word. When Herod meant to kill him, “earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church” (Acts 12:5), and in the night an angel led him out. He knew what stretched-out love could do. He asks not for warm feeling but for love that costs something to sustain.

A realistic command. These congregations were thrown together by nothing except Christ: slaves and masters in one room, people with notorious pasts beside former synagogue-goers. Loving them would not happen by temperament; it needed the love the Spirit pours into hearts (Romans 5:5).

As I have loved you. Peter is passing on a command he first heard with wet feet. On the night before the cross Jesus washed the feet of all twelve, Peter protesting, Judas included, and said: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another” (John 13:34). The measure is Christ’s own love, and its proof the cross a few hours later. So brotherly love in the church is not a social nicety but the family likeness of people washed by the same Lord, and “by this all people will know that you are my disciples” (John 13:35).

What if there is someone in my church I find very hard to love? Then this verse was written for you. Peter is not asking you to like everyone equally, but to do them good, earnestly, from the heart. Pray for them by name; it is very hard to keep resenting someone you regularly bring to God for blessing. Do one concrete kind thing, and speak well of them when they are absent. If there is a real wrong between you, seek to put it right (Matthew 18:15). Feelings often follow actions, but the command does not wait for them.

Does loving earnestly mean I must tolerate sin? No. Love “rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6), and sometimes requires loving correction, church discipline or protecting the vulnerable. Earnest love is not soft; it wants the other’s good, which can mean saying hard things or refusing to enable harm. What it rules out is coldness, gossip, cliques, and the polite distance that keeps fellow believers at arm’s length while appearing friendly.

verseByVerse.quote: since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are one family because God gave them new life through his word, a seed that cannot die, so their family can never be dissolved.

Since you have been born again. The reason under the command goes back to verse 3. They are brothers because God gave them the same new birth, not because they chose one another, which is why love is commanded and not left to whether they get on. You do not choose your siblings.

Imperishable seed. Seed (spora): sowing, origin. Imperishable for the third time: the inheritance (v. 4), the ransom not paid in perishable silver (v. 18), and now the seed. Natural birth uses seed that dies, and nearly everyone in that congregation had buried somebody. This birth does not, so the family it creates cannot be dissolved by what dissolves every other family. Death parts husbands and wives, parents and children. It cannot part brothers and sisters in Christ, because the life they share is the life of the risen Christ, through whose resurrection they were born again (v. 3), and who “will never die again” (Romans 6:9).

The living and abiding word of God. The seed is the word, as the Sower himself explained to Peter: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11). Living: it generates life (Hebrews 4:12). Abiding: it will still be there when everything visible has gone. God gives new birth (v. 3; John 3:8), and he does it through the gospel preached: “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth” (James 1:18). The Spirit uses the word as his instrument, which is why the church preaches.

Not with seed that dies. He spoke, and by his living word, carried by his Spirit, dead hearts in Cappadocia and in our own street woke up and called him Father. The family he has created will stand round his throne when every other family on earth has gone to dust.

In everyday life. Look around your church next Sunday: these are not people I chose; they are people God fathered by the same word that fathered me, and they will be my family for ever. Then pick one you hardly know and find out one thing about them.

Does this mean baptism gives new birth? No. The seed Peter names is the word of God, the gospel preached, not the water of baptism. Baptism is the sign and confession of a new birth already given through the word and Spirit, which is why it belongs to those who believe. When Peter does speak of baptism (3:21), he insists that it is not the washing of the body that saves, but the appeal of a good conscience to God through the resurrection. Christians who baptise infants also deny that the water itself regenerates; we differ with them on who should receive the sign, not on how new birth comes.

Why does it matter that the word is living? Because when you read or hear Scripture you are not handling a museum piece. The word that gave you life goes on feeding it (2:2), and can convict, comfort, correct and change you today, because God is speaking in it. That is why a Christian who neglects it grows weak, and why a sermon is never only information. Come to the word expecting God to do something.

Uncertain wording. “Living and abiding” could describe the word, as in the ESV, or God: the word of the living and abiding God (compare Daniel 6:26, “the living God, enduring forever”). Verse 25, “the word of the Lord remains forever”, makes the ESV’s reading more likely: Peter is speaking of the word that remains. And since the word is God’s, what is true of him is true of it.

verseByVerse.quote: for "All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever." And this word is the good news that was preached to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything human, its glory included, withers like grass, but the word of the Lord lasts for ever, and that word is the gospel these believers heard.

All flesh is like grass. Isaiah 40 speaks to exiles wondering whether God had finished with them: “Comfort, comfort my people” (Isaiah 40:1). Not only the grass but “all its glory” withers: beauty, power, wealth, fame.

The grass withers. The picture James also used (James 1:10–11): the hills of Israel green after the winter rains and carpeted with wildflowers, then the hot wind off the eastern desert browning the landscape within a day. Peter writes to people outranked by neighbours with standing, and Isaiah’s word is that standing is the most temporary thing about them. The magistrates who fined them, the families who disowned them, Rome with all its marble, are wildflowers on a hillside, and the wind is coming. That is hard for anyone set on being admired, and freeing: if all human glory withers, mine included, I no longer have to win the approval I was so afraid of losing.

Remains forever. The contrast the whole chapter has been leading to. Remains (menei), abides, is the root of “abiding” in verse 23: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). In Isaiah this comforted exiles in Babylon: empires rise and fall, but God’s promise stands. Babylon fell, Persia fell, Greece fell, and the word of the Lord did not. Set the imperishable seed beside the withering flower and you have Peter’s whole view of his readers’ situation.

The good news that was preached to you. Preached as good news (euangelisthen). Isaiah’s eternal word is not far off and vague. It is the message somebody, perhaps a travelling trader, brought to Pontus and Cappadocia and said out loud in a room, and these readers believed it. That gives ordinary preaching a remarkable dignity: the word that outlasts all flesh is the seed that gave them a birth that cannot perish.

The chapter that opens the Gospels. All four Gospels use Isaiah 40 to introduce John the Baptist: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isaiah 40:3; Mark 1:3; John 1:23). And Isaiah 40 says what the good news is. The herald cries to the cities of Judah, “Behold your God!” (40:9), the God who comes with might and yet tends his flock like a shepherd and gathers the lambs in his arms (40:10–11). That God came. The word that outlasts all flesh is the news that the Lord himself arrived in Jesus, took the frail flesh Isaiah calls grass, died in it, and rose in it never to wither again.

In everyday life. Walk past something impressive today, a tall office building or a famous name, and say quietly: flower of grass. Then thank God for the ordinary person who first told you the gospel.

If everything withers, why work hard at anything? Because “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Your job, family and service are not worthless because they are temporary; done for Christ, they are joined to his eternal purposes. What withers is the glory, the vanity of building a name for yourself. What lasts is the person you are becoming, the people you have loved into the kingdom, and the word you have passed on. Work hard, but do not build your identity on what the wind will take.

How is the gospel the word of the Lord when ordinary people speak it? God speaks through his messengers when they speak his message. Faithfully preached, the gospel is not human opinion about God but the word of God at work in those who believe (1 Thessalonians 2:13). The preacher may be unimpressive and the room small, but the word is the one Isaiah heard. So listen to faithful preaching with expectation. Every believer who shares the gospel with a friend hands on something that will outlast the stars.
