keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
keyVerse.note: This verse is the root from which the whole chapter grows. The joy in trials, the call to hope, holiness and love, all rest on what God has already done: he has given new life and a hope as sure as the empty tomb. And it begins, as the Christian life must, with blessing God rather than with our troubles.

1.reflection:
Peter calls his readers “elect exiles” (v. 1). Where do you most feel out of place because you follow Christ? How does it change things to see that as the experience of someone chosen, not rejected?

Verses 6–7 say that trials last “for a little while”, come only “if necessary”, and refine something more precious than gold. Which of these do you find hardest to believe about your own troubles, and why?

Every command in verses 13–25 rests on something God has already done. Choose one (hope, holiness, reverent fear or love) and trace it back to its reason in the chapter. How does the reason change the way you obey?

Peter says you were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (vv. 18–19). What does that price say about your worth to God, and about the believers you find hardest to love (v. 22)?

2.title: Living Stones and Holy Exiles: Identity, Witness, and the Suffering Christ
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 is the hinge of the letter: verses 1–10 finish Peter’s account of who believers are, and verse 11 opens the long middle section (2:11–4:11) on how they live among neighbours who do not understand them.

The message. You were nobody, and in Christ God has made you his own people: a living temple built on the stone men rejected and God chose, a royal priesthood, his treasured possession. So live among those who slander you as free servants of God: do good, accept human authority for the Lord’s sake, and bear unjust suffering as Christ did, who bore your sins. Who they are shapes how they live, and how they live shows their neighbours who they are.

Why it was said. The readers had no temple, priesthood or standing; neighbours called them evildoers, and many were slaves whose masters could beat them at will (see the introduction). They might conclude that they really were nothing, or answer contempt with contempt, revolt or revenge.

How the chapter makes its case. First their identity: newborns crave the word (vv. 1–3); coming to Christ, the living stone, they are built into one house and priesthood (vv. 4–5); three stone texts show that his rejection was foretold and that everyone builds on him or falls over him (vv. 6–8); and Israel’s titles are given to them by mercy (vv. 9–10). Then their conduct: fight the desires within and live so well that slanderers end up glorifying God (vv. 11–12); accept the authority of emperor and governors for the Lord’s sake, as free servants of God (vv. 13–17); and, for slaves, serve even harsh masters, for unjust suffering borne with God in view is precious to him (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. Both halves meet in Christ. The stone men rejected and God chose (v. 4) is the Servant who was reviled and did not revile in return, but handed his case to the Judge (vv. 22–23); Peter, who once drew a sword in the garden, had watched it. Christ’s steps are a pattern to trace (v. 21), but verse 24 goes where no follower can: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.” And the Shepherd brought the straying sheep home (v. 25).

For us. If you feel like nobody, God has named you. If you are treated unfairly with no way to put it right, you walk where your Lord walked: do good, refuse revenge, and hand your case to the God who judges justly. And the one you follow first carried your sins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You are no longer nobodies: in Christ you are God’s own house and priesthood, so grow up into it. Born again by the word, they must put away what poisons love and crave that word like newborns (vv. 1–3). Coming to Christ, the living stone men rejected and God chose, they are built together into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood (vv. 4–5). Scripture foretold that this stone would be a sure foundation for believers and a stumbling stone for unbelievers (vv. 6–8). And every title God gave Israel at Sinai now belongs to them, given by mercy so that they may proclaim his excellencies (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priesthood of All Believers

Coming to Christ, the living stone, believers are built into one spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel’s titles were given to Gentile converts with no status at all.

Now: Once not a people, now God’s people; once without mercy, now shown mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Born again by the word, believers should strip off the sins that poison love and crave God’s word as a newborn craves milk. The appetite rests on a taste they have already had: the kindness of the Lord.

So put away all malice. Because you have been born again (1:22–23), strip it off like clothing (James 1:21): these are the garments of the old family, and they no longer fit. Malice is ill will, the inner wickedness from which the rest grows.

Deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander. Every one is a sin against other people, done mostly with words or with a face: the list of what makes the earnest love of 1:22 impossible. Deceit (dolos) is the bait that hides the hook. Hypocrisy is the actor’s mask, the opposite of the “sincere” (literally un-hypocritical) love of 1:22. Envy resents another’s good. Slander, backbiting (James 4:11), was exactly what these readers suffered from outside (2:12), and Peter will not let a slandered congregation do the same to one another. Note “all”, three times: a church cannot have a little backbiting.

Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk. Newly born people should have an appetite. Long for is a strong verb, crave: the noise a hungry baby makes, which is not a polite request. A newborn wants milk with its whole body and will not be distracted by a rattle. The milk is the word that gave them birth (1:23–25; see the wording note below). Pure (adolon) plays on the deceit (dolon) of verse 1: put off the deceit; drink the milk with no deceit in it.

Grow up into salvation. Elsewhere milk is the beginner’s diet (Hebrews 5:12–13); here it is the food that produces growth, and the diet never changes. The oldest saint is as dependent on the word as the newest convert, and should be as hungry.

If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good. Psalm 34:8: “Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good!”, a psalm Peter returns to (3:10–12). Appetite follows a taste: people who have truly tasted something good need no persuading to want more. Good (chrēstos), kind, sounds almost exactly like Christos, and Peter may intend the echo.

The LORD David tasted has a name. In Psalm 34 the Lord is Yahweh, whom David tasted as a fugitive. Peter applies the words without comment to Christ, the living stone of the next verse, as though it were obvious that the LORD of David’s psalm is Jesus. We tasted his kindness the day we first understood that his blood was for us, and taste it whenever his word lands on a weary heart like milk on a hungry child, at his table now and at his feast for ever.

What if I have no appetite for the Bible? Do what a doctor would advise for a child who has stopped eating: find what is spoiling the appetite, and keep offering the food. Peter puts the two together: put away the sins, and crave the milk. Unconfessed sin, a grudge or constant distraction kills spiritual hunger; confess them. Then read a little, regularly, asking God to show you Christ there, starting with the Gospels if the rest is hard. Appetite often returns by eating, and the God who caused you to be born again gives his children hunger.

How do I actually put off slander and envy? Name them and replace them. Catch the sentence that begins “Have you heard about…”, and stop it. When someone is praised and something in you shrinks, call it envy and thank God for that person instead. Say nothing you would not say with the person in the room, and take a real grievance to the person, not to others (Matthew 18:15). You strip off old clothes because you have new ones: Christ’s love for you leaves no need to diminish anyone else.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “spiritual” (logikon) appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in Romans 12:1, of our “spiritual worship” (or reasonable, rational). It is related to logos, word, and older translations read the sincere milk of the word. It is not certain whether Peter means milk of the word or milk that is spiritual rather than literal. Since he has just said they were born “through the living and abiding word of God” (1:23), the likely meaning holds both: the nourishment is God’s word, and it feeds the inner life.

verseByVerse.quote: As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers keep coming to Christ, the living stone men rejected and God chose, and God builds them together into his temple and priesthood. Their offerings are acceptable to God because they come through Jesus Christ.

As you come to him. The picture changes from infancy to masonry. Come is the word for drawing near to God in worship (Hebrews 4:16), and the present tense means keep coming. It probably still echoes Psalm 34, which in the Greek version Peter’s readers used goes on, come to him and be enlightened (Psalm 34:5).

A living stone rejected by men. Stone is the deadest material there is, and Peter calls it living, as he called hope (1:3) and the word (1:23): this stone is alive because he has risen. Rejected is a builder’s word, tested and declared unfit (Psalm 118:22). The religious leaders examined Jesus, cross-questioned him, tried him and threw him out (Mark 8:31; 12:10).

Chosen and precious. From Isaiah 28:16, applied first to Christ: two verdicts on the same person. Men rejected him; God chose and honoured him. The readers, rejected in Pontus, are being told which verdict counts.

You yourselves like living stones. Peter’s name means rock, and if anyone could have claimed to be the foundation stone, it was he. He does not. Christ is the living stone, and Peter is one stone among many, the slave and the apostle alike.

Are being built up as a spiritual house. God is the builder, still at work, and Peter says a house, not houses: a temple made of people and indwelt by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Corinthians 3:16). The temple in Jerusalem, of dead stones, would soon be thrown down; God’s temple of living people will never fall. A stone on its own is rubble; it becomes masonry only when set against other stones. Scattered, isolated believers are load-bearing parts of one building.

The quarry and the chisel. A stone is cut out of the rock, shaped until it fits, and set next to stones it did not choose; every Christian knows all three. The Builder is not making separate statues but a house for himself to live in.

To be a holy priesthood. Not some believers, but all: the root of what the Reformers called the priesthood of all believers. In the temple ordinary Israelites stood in the outer courts while the priests went in; now the congregation is itself the building, the priesthood and the offerers (Revelation 1:6). Where one man entered the Most Holy Place once a year, a whole people, slaves and fishermen and housewives, now come boldly to the throne of grace every day.

Spiritual sacrifices. Not animals, but praise, “the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15); doing good and sharing what we have (Hebrews 13:16); our bodies given to God as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1); gifts for the gospel (Philippians 4:18); prayer (Revelation 8:3–4); and declaring his excellencies (v. 9). Acceptable means well-pleasing.

Through Jesus Christ. The last words leave no room for pride: even the offerings of a priesthood need a mediator. Our praise is stained and our good works are mixed. But Christ offered God a perfect obedience in our place, and so God receives our offerings gladly, because they come to him through the hands of his Son, our one great High Priest.

In everyday life. You are a priest today: the sink, the desk, the hospital ward and the steering wheel are altars. Offer praise aloud in the car, your work as done for him, a gift to someone in need.

How do I keep coming to him? Coming to Christ is not only the first step of faith but the shape of the whole Christian life, and it looks very ordinary. Come first thing. Before the phone and the news, a few verses and a sentence of prayer: Lord, I come to you again. Come with what you have. Bring the guilt, the worry and the unfinished work: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Come by his word. Read the Gospels listening for him, not only for information. Come with his people. Sunday by Sunday the church comes to him as one house. And notice who moved first: the stone was laid for you before you took a step, so every return, even after a fall, is not a fresh application but a coming home.

Can I be a Christian without a church? Not in any healthy sense. A living stone is not meant to lie in a field: Christ saves individuals into a house, and the New Testament knows nothing of believers who refuse to belong to a local congregation. If a church has hurt you, that is real and grievous, and you may need time and care; but the answer is a better church, not no church. Find one that preaches Christ faithfully, commit to it, and let yourself be set in the wall, rough edges and all.

If every believer is a priest, is there any place for ordained ministers? Yes, though not as a priestly class (see the box below). The New Testament gives elders to teach and shepherd the church (5:1–4). They are not priests between God and his people, but servants of the word among a priestly people.

Where Christians differ: is there a special priesthood in the church? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches maintain an ordained priesthood that offers sacrifice on behalf of the people. This commentary’s view: The New Testament teaches the priesthood of all believers. Every Christian is a priest, offering spiritual sacrifices directly to God through Christ, the one great High Priest. The church has elders and deacons, who lead and serve, but no priestly caste that mediates between God and the people (1 Timothy 2:5). Peter himself, the first leader of the apostles, calls himself a fellow elder (5:1), and Christ, not Peter, the stone on which the church is built.

verseByVerse.quote: For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," and "A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture foretold that God would lay Christ as the stone on which believers build and over which unbelievers fall. His rejection does not disprove his claims; it fulfils them.

For it stands in Scripture. Three Old Testament texts about a stone make one point: the rejection of Jesus was not a surprise the apostles had to explain away. It was written.

A cornerstone chosen and precious. Isaiah 28:16. The cornerstone set the lines of the whole building. When Jerusalem trusted in alliances with Egypt, God said, I am laying a stone of my own.

Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. In the Greek translation of Isaiah the stone is a person, someone to believe in (Romans 9:33). The readers’ neighbours were shaming them; God promises that the shame will not stick.

So the honor is for you who believe. The honour God gives the stone is shared with those who rest on it. The people the world dishonours are joined to the stone God honours (see the note on the wording below).

The stone that the builders rejected. Psalm 118:22. The Lord quoted it of himself (Matthew 21:42), and Peter quoted it before the Sanhedrin to the very builders who had done the rejecting (Acts 4:11).

A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense. Isaiah 8:14, and the picture changes on purpose: the stone to build on becomes a stone to trip over. Offence is skandalon, a trap, a cause of falling. Nothing about the stone changes; what differs is whether a man builds on it or trips over it (1 Corinthians 1:23). And no one can simply walk past it. It is set in the middle of the road of every human life: you will either build on Christ or fall over him.

They stumble because they disobey the word. Disobey means refuse to be persuaded, for the gospel commands repentance and faith. Peter gives this reason first: a real refusal, genuinely theirs.

As they were destined to do. Their own guilty choice, within God’s sovereign purpose: Peter softens neither half, and does not make God the author of the disobedience. Christians differ over how far the appointment reaches (see the box below), but either way the stumbling is their own act. No one in hell will be able to say that he wanted Christ and was refused.

Still he stands. Unbelief cannot overturn God’s choice. The builders of this world have thrown Christ off the site a thousand times, and every time God has set him back at the head of the corner. Empires have stumbled over him and lie in pieces; philosophies have broken on him; and still he stands.

In everyday life. Where does Christ still offend you: a command, a doctrine, a claim that embarrasses you in front of friends? That is where you are tempted to stumble rather than build. Bring it to him.

Is it presumptuous to say everyone must either build on Christ or fall over him? Only if Christians had invented the claim or thought themselves better for believing it. But the claim is Christ’s (John 14:6), and those who repeat it once tripped over him and were picked up by mercy. Every view of the world says some people are wrong; the question is whether it is true. And the stone is laid for whoever believes, respectable or ruined; the only people kept out are those who refuse to build. A narrow door is not arrogant if it is the only door and stands open.

Should this make me worry that I or someone I love is destined to stumble? No. The verse is not given to make anyone search God’s secret decree, but to explain why so many reject Christ and to steady puzzled believers. If you fear stumbling, come to him now: whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. For those you love, keep praying and speaking; you do not know who is chosen. Saul of Tarsus stumbled over this stone for years, then was knocked down by it on the Damascus road and rose a believer.

Where Christians differ: does God destine people to unbelief? Some read this as teaching only that God appointed the consequence (stumbling) for those who freely choose to disobey. This commentary’s view: The verse teaches that those who disobey stumble according to God’s appointment. God is sovereign over all things, including the rejection of Christ by unbelievers (Romans 9:18–22; Acts 4:27–28). Yet the stumbling is caused by their own disobedience, for which they are wholly responsible. God passes over some, leaving them in their sin, and justly appoints them to its consequences; he does not create unbelief in an innocent heart. The doctrine is to be handled with humility and reverence, not speculation, and it is set against the glory of the chosen in the next verse.

Uncertain wording. The opening of verse 7 is compressed in Greek: literally, to you therefore the honour (or preciousness), who believe. Older translations read, to you who believe he is precious; most modern ones, like the ESV, give the honour to believers. The word picks up “precious” in verse 6 and answers “will not be put to shame”, so the likely meaning is that believers share the honour of the stone God honours. Both readings say true things.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every title God gave Israel now belongs to the church, given by mercy to people who were nobody, so that they may tell of the God who called them into his light.

But you are a chosen race. “But you”: the contrast with the stumblers is total. Four titles follow, every one lifted from what God said to Israel, most of it at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Isaiah 43:20–21). A chosen race is a people made not by descent but by God’s choice. Imagine hearing it read aloud: people of little account, with no priesthood, no nation and few possessions, told they are a race, a priesthood, a nation and a treasured possession.

A royal priesthood. From Exodus 19:6, “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests”: priests who belong to the King and share his reign (Revelation 1:6; 5:10). In Israel kings and priests were kept strictly apart; when King Uzziah burned incense in the temple, he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The one clear Old Testament figure who was both is the mysterious Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18), and the Messiah was promised to be a priest for ever after his order (Psalm 110:4). Christ is that King-Priest, and in him his people are both.

A holy nation. A nation without borders, army or earthly capital, drawn from every nation, and the only one that will last for ever.

A people for his own possession. A king’s private treasure: the Hebrew word behind it in Exodus 19:5 (segullah) is used of one (1 Chronicles 29:3). People whom Rome counted as nobody are the crown jewels of the King of heaven.

That you may proclaim the excellencies. Tell out his mighty deeds (Isaiah 43:21). The whole congregation is given this work: the titles are not for admiring themselves but for telling others how great God is.

Him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Called means God’s effectual call: not an invitation that might be refused but the summons that brings a person to life and faith, as Jesus’ call brought Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43). The darkness is ignorance, sin and the realm of Satan (Acts 26:18; Colossians 1:13). Conversion is a move from one realm into another, like the exodus out of Egypt’s darkness. And the light is marvellous: Christians who have walked in it for fifty years are still astonished.

Once you were not a people. Hosea named his children Not My People and No Mercy, and God promised to reverse the names (Hosea 1:6–10; 2:23). Peter, like Paul (Romans 9:25–26), applies the reversal to Gentiles who never had the names in the first place. Whatever these readers are being called in Pontus, their name has already been changed once, and the God who changed it does not change it back.

Every title was his first. Christ is the chosen stone (v. 4), the King who is also Priest, the Holy One of God, the beloved Son in whom the Father delights. These people are chosen because they are in the Chosen One, and everything God says of them he first said of him. Chosen, royal, holy, treasured: every title is a gift, every gift is mercy, and every mercy was bought with blood.

How do I proclaim his excellencies if I am not a preacher? By speaking naturally of what God has done for you. Tell a friend what you are thankful for and why; when someone asks why you are different, say what Christ means to you; sing in church as if you meant it; pray aloud with a struggling neighbour; live so that people ask (3:15). His excellencies are not a script for professionals but the testimony of everyone brought out of darkness who still remembers what it was like.

I struggle with low self-worth. How does this help? It gives you a name that does not depend on how you feel, what others say or how you did this week. God calls you chosen, royal, holy, treasured, and says it to people who were once nobody. Your worth is not something to build; he has declared it and paid for it. That makes you no better than anyone, for all of it is mercy, but the voices calling you worthless are lying. Answer them with God’s words: once I was not a people, now I am God’s people; once I had not received mercy, now I have.

Has the church replaced Israel? There is one people of God, and its centre is Christ (see the box below).

Where Christians differ: is the church a replacement for Israel, or are they two separate peoples? Dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, and who expect God to fulfil his promises to ethnic Israel separately from the church) keep Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with distinct promises; some speak of replacement theology, in which the church replaces Israel entirely. This commentary’s view: Peter applies Israel’s titles directly to the mostly Gentile church. The church is not a separate people from Israel but the fulfilment of God’s purpose for Israel: one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, the true seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22; Romans 11:17–24). This is fulfilment, not mere replacement: believing Jews were the core of the church, and God continues to graft Jews back in through faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26).
verseByVerse.note: Titles once given to Israel at Sinai are now given to the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — Submission, and the Steps of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Exiles show whose they are by how they live among those who slander them, and Christ’s unjust suffering is both their pattern and their salvation. Peter calls them to fight the desires within and live so well that slanderers may glorify God (vv. 11–12); to accept the authority of emperor and governors for the Lord’s sake, as free people who serve God (vv. 13–17); and, for slaves, to serve even unjust masters with God in view (vv. 18–20). The ground of it all is Christ, who suffered unjustly without retaliation, entrusted himself to the just Judge, bore our sins in his body on the tree, and brought straying sheep home (vv. 21–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Entrusting Rather Than Suppressing

Christ did not revile in return; he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly. Then he did what no follower can copy: he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter spoke directly to slaves, and told believers to honour an emperor who would soon persecute them.

Now: Follow in his steps: do good, refuse revenge (which never means staying in danger), and hand the case to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they belong to God and not to this world, believers must fight the desires that war against their souls and live such good lives that some who slander them will end up glorifying God.

Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles. Peter does not lecture strangers; he pleads with people he loves. The words of 1:1 and 1:17 now become the reason for how they live: you do not belong here, so do not live like those who do.

Abstain from the passions of the flesh. Abstain means keep away from. The passions of the flesh are the desires of fallen nature turned in on itself (Galatians 5:19–21), not the body, which God made and will raise.

Which wage war against your soul. To campaign as soldiers (James 4:1). Here is a nearer enemy than the neighbours, inside the walls, campaigning against the very soul whose salvation Peter has described (1:9). Sinful desire presents itself as a friend; Peter shows it to be an enemy soldier.

Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable. Gentiles here means unbelievers: Peter so fully counts his Gentile readers as God’s people that their old name now belongs to outsiders. Honourable means good, even beautiful: not merely correct but attractive.

When they speak against you as evildoers. When, not if: the slander is assumed, and it is the word of verse 1. Early Christians were accused of atheism, having no gods or images; of cannibalism, from rumours of eating a body and drinking blood at the Lord’s Supper; of incest, since they called each other brother and sister and greeted with a kiss; and of disloyalty, since they would not worship the emperor. They were bad for business too.

What Pliny found. Some fifty years later Pliny, governor of these very provinces of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan that with the spread of the Christians the temples had been almost deserted and buyers for sacrificial meat had grown scarce. He tortured two slave women whom the Christians called deaconesses, and found nothing but what he called a perverse and excessive superstition; the Christians, he reported, bound themselves by oath not to steal, commit adultery or break their word. Even the persecutor found no evidence for the worst of the slanders.

They may see your good deeds. See means watch over time, as neighbours do who are trying to find something wrong. The plan is not to win arguments but to live where it can be seen: “let your light shine before others” (Matthew 5:16). The aim is not the believers’ reputation but that their accusers glorify God (see the wording note below).

He was called an evildoer before them. The slander had been aimed at their Lord first. His accusers told Pilate he was doing evil (John 18:30); he was condemned as an evildoer and hung between two of them, and his life answered the charge. He did not argue his way out of the slander; he loved his way through it, and on the third day God vindicated him.

How do I fight a desire that feels overwhelming? As an enemy, not a part of you to negotiate with. Abstain means keep away, so do not stand near the fire: remove the apps, change the route, avoid being alone with the bottle or the person. Tell a trusted Christian friend; sin grows in the dark and shrinks in the light. When the desire comes, turn your mind to Christ and what is promised (1:13): a greater love expels a lesser one. When you fall, confess, receive forgiveness and get up. The soldier who falls is not the one who loses; the one who changes sides is.

What if people speak badly of me even though I am doing good? Then you are in good company, and Peter wrote this letter for you. Keep doing good, without bitterness, and let your life do the talking. You may calmly correct a false accusation, but leave the verdict to God and to the slow work of evidence. Many who slandered Christians in one decade were Christians in the next, and your patience may be what God uses to bring them.

Uncertain wording. The day of visitation (hēmera episkopēs) is a day when God comes, whether to save (Luke 19:44) or to judge (Isaiah 10:3), and Peter does not say which. Some read it as the day of judgment, when even unbelievers must acknowledge that God’s people were right. More likely, pagans who have watched Christians’ good deeds will be converted and glorify God when he visits them in mercy. So good lives can win slanderers to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Lord’s sake, Christians accept the authority of rulers, because God gives government to restrain evil and because good citizens silence slander against the gospel. “For the Lord’s sake” gives both the reason for this submission and its limit.

Be subject for the Lord’s sake. To be subject is to take your place willingly in an order God has made (2:18; 3:1), here law and government (Romans 13:1–7). “For the Lord’s sake” means do it for my sake: as you might care for a friend’s elderly father while he is abroad, really helping the father, but doing it for your friend (see on Ephesians 5:22, and As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary). Not because every official deserves it, nor merely to avoid being caught, but because the Lord who ransomed us asks it, and law-abiding Christians make the gospel believable (v. 15). And what is done for the Lord’s sake can never include what the Lord forbids.

To every human institution. Monarchy or parliament: human in form, ordained by God in existence (Romans 13:1; see the wording note below). On leadership and submission in every sphere, from the home to the state, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Whether it be to the emperor as supreme. Remember who the emperor was. The letter was most likely written in the early 60s, so the man called supreme was Nero, who within a few years would use Christians as living torches in his gardens, as the Roman historian Tacitus records, and under whom, by early tradition, Peter himself would die. That should govern how the verse is read. Peter is not describing an ideal government or making submission depend on the ruler’s good behaviour; he is telling a persecuted minority to be model subjects of a ruler who will kill them.

Or to governors as sent by him. Men like Pilate, Felix and Festus, and later Pliny in Bithynia. Peter knew such men: a governor had sent his Lord to the cross.

To punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. The function is justice (Romans 13:3–4), and Peter, flogged by the council (Acts 5:40), states it anyway: he describes the office, not flattering its holders. A world with corrupt police is still safer than one with none.

Put to silence the ignorance of foolish people. Muzzle, as one muzzles an ox. The best answer to slander is a life that leaves it nothing to work with.

The King behind the emperor. Christ himself submitted to a corrupt high priest’s court and to Pilate’s, for his Father’s sake. Nero had his day, and his gardens are dust; the Lord he persecuted reigns, King of kings. So we can submit to rulers without fear, because they are not the last authority, and defy them without hatred when we must, because their power was given from above.

The apostle who disobeyed. Ordered to stop preaching, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), and took the beating rejoicing (Acts 5:41). The pattern is Daniel at his open window: respectful, unbending, and willing to pay.

What about a government I believe is wicked? Peter’s readers had one, and his instruction did not change. You may disagree with your rulers, vote against them, protest lawfully and speak the truth about them; you must still pray for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), pay your taxes, obey just laws and refuse to speak of them with contempt. The limit is not whether you like them but whether they command you to sin; then you obey God, openly and peaceably, and accept the cost. A Christian’s politics should show more respect, more prayer and less rage than his neighbour’s, because he knows who is really on the throne.

Where Christians differ: when may Christians disobey the government? This commentary’s view: Christians must submit to governing authorities as a general rule, paying taxes, obeying laws and honouring officials (Romans 13:1–7). But when the government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, believers must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19–20; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Even then, they should accept the consequences peacefully, without violent rebellion, as Peter and the apostles did. Christians may also work through lawful means to change unjust laws.

Uncertain wording. “Every human institution” is literally every human creation (ktisis), a word that elsewhere means creation or creature and is never used of an institution. Some therefore read every human creature, that is, everyone, which would fit “Honor everyone” (v. 17). But the emperor and governors who follow make it most likely that Peter means the structures of authority among people, human in their forms but ordained by God.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor at the time was probably Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians are truly free, but free as God’s servants. Their freedom is never an excuse for evil; it shows itself in honouring everyone, loving fellow believers, fearing God alone and respecting the ruler.

Live as people who are free. An extraordinary thing to say to people told to submit to Nero, and to slaves two verses later. The freedom is not political but freedom from sin’s slavery, the law’s condemnation, and the fear of man and of death (John 8:36; Galatians 5:1).

Not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil. A cover thrown over what is underneath: claiming freedom in Christ as an excuse for wrong (Galatians 5:13). A freedom used to do evil has already become a new slavery.

But living as servants of God. Free, and yet slaves of God: the two belong together (Romans 6:22). A man wholly owned by God is beyond the reach of anyone else’s ownership, which is why the slave of verse 18 can be told he is free. A fish is free in water, not out of it; we are free only when we belong to the God we were made for.

The sons are free. Peter had learned this freedom at Capernaum, when the collectors of the temple tax asked whether his teacher paid it. From whom do kings take tax, Jesus asked, their sons or others? From others, said Peter. “Then the sons are free”; yet, so as not to give offence, Peter was to find a coin in a fish’s mouth and pay “for me and for yourself” (Matthew 17:24–27). There is verse 16 in a story: the Son of the King, owing nothing, paying anyway, and including Peter in his freedom. Christians submit as free sons, and the Son pays their way.

Honor everyone. First and universal: every human being, made in God’s image, slaves, pagans and slandering neighbours included. In a rigidly stratified society that was close to revolutionary.

Love the brotherhood. Fear God. A narrower circle and a warmer word: respect for all, love for the family. Fear belongs to one being only (Proverbs 1:7). He alone is to be feared, because he alone is God, and the one who fears him need fear nothing else.

Honor the emperor. The emperor gets the same verb as everyone else, honour, not the verb kept for God, fear. Where emperors were called divine and incense was burned to them, that is a carefully weighed sentence: Christians would respect him as a ruler but not worship him as a god. Caesar is worth exactly as much honour as the man who cleans his stables, and not one degree of the fear that belongs to God. “My son, fear the LORD and the king” (Proverbs 24:21); “render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21).

In everyday life. Ask a question about fear as well as honour: is there anyone you fear more than God? That is the fear that makes you less free, and the Son has already paid your way.

How can I honour someone I find contemptible? Honour is given for what a person is before God, not for how he behaves: every human being bears God’s image, however defaced, and every ruler holds an office God has made. You can oppose a policy, even refuse an unjust order, and still refuse to mock, sneer or dehumanise. Honour looks like courtesy in speech, fairness in description, prayer for the person, and no gloating at his downfall. If Peter could honour Nero, we can honour our opponents.

verseByVerse.quote: Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian slaves were to serve their masters respectfully, even harsh ones, because enduring unjust suffering with God in view is precious to him. Peter is not endorsing slavery or abuse (see the questions below); he is showing the powerless how to live before God.

Servants, be subject to your masters. Household slaves, not employees: a large part of those cities was enslaved (see Slavery in the Ancient World), and many early believers were slaves. Respect is literally fear, very probably reverence towards God shown in how they serve. On leading and following at work and elsewhere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Peter speaks to slaves. He addresses them directly, as moral agents with choices to make. Greek and Roman household codes did not normally do that: slaves were property, Aristotle’s living tools, and you addressed their owners. Simply by speaking to them, Peter gives them a dignity their culture denied. He gives no matching word to masters, as Paul does (Ephesians 6:9), perhaps because few belonged to these churches, or because his concern is suffering under unjust authority. He writes to the bottom of the ladder, and gives it the longest passage in the chapter and the fullest picture of Christ.

Not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. Unjust (skoliois) is crooked (our word scoliosis). The slave had no appeal against such a master, and Peter does not pretend otherwise.

For this is a gracious thing. Literally, this is grace: something of God’s own favour is present in that endurance.

When, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. Literally, because of conscience towards God. What makes it grace is not the suffering, which by itself is merely misfortune, but that the sufferer holds God in view while it happens. Peter is not praising endurance for its own sake.

For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? Beaten means struck with the fist, the word used of the blows Jesus received in the high priest’s house (Matthew 26:67). The sharp line keeps the teaching honest: bearing quietly a punishment you deserved earns no praise. The grace is in enduring what you did not deserve.

In the sight of God. The master may never notice, but the slave’s patience is seen in heaven.

The lowest place is now holy ground. God sent his Son in the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7), to be struck with fists and to die the death reserved for slaves. The Lord of glory took the lowest place, and so it is now holy ground.

In everyday life. If you face unfair treatment at work this week, ask before you react: am I mindful of God right now? And be honest about the other half of Peter’s distinction: if the trouble is my own fault, I need to repent, not to feel noble.

Does this mean the Bible approves of slavery? Peter addresses believers as they actually were, without endorsing the system, and Scripture lays the seeds of its overthrow: a slave is a beloved brother (Philemon 16), slaves should gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and enslavers are listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Every human being bears God’s image, and slave and master stand equal before Christ (Galatians 3:28). Christians reading their Bibles led many of the campaigns that ended the slave trade. Other professing Christians, honesty requires adding, defended slavery from the same Bible; but the slavery of the Americas was built on kidnapping, the man-stealing the law punished with death (Exodus 21:16), and Peter’s words give it no cover.

Must a Christian employee today simply endure abuse? A modern employee is not a slave: he can leave, seek legal protection and report wrongdoing. The principle still applies: work well, honour those over you even when they are unfair, and do not repay evil with evil. But nothing here requires anyone to stay in an abusive situation or cover up a crime.

What if I am being harmed at home? Hear this clearly: this passage is not a command to stay in danger. Peter is addressing slaves who had no legal way out; you are not, and the apostles themselves used the protection of the law (Acts 16:37). Abuse is a sin that God hates, and the church must never tolerate it or counsel anyone to endure it silently. Tell someone you trust, contact your church leaders and, if you are at risk, the police or an abuse support service. Seeking safety is not a failure of faith. What Peter forbids is revenge, not protection.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suffering unjustly for doing good is part of the Christian calling, because Christ suffered for us and left us a pattern to trace.

For to this you have been called. A hard sentence, and it needs care. “To this” means to patient endurance of unjust suffering, and called is the word Peter used of their calling out of darkness into marvellous light (2:9): one calling with two sides, into his light and into suffering for doing good. “It has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake” (Philippians 1:29; 2 Timothy 3:12).

Because Christ also suffered for you. “For you” means in our place first of all (v. 24); only then is his suffering an example. A servant who suffers unjustly walks where his Lord walked.

Leaving you an example. Example (hypogrammos) is the schoolmaster’s copybook line: letters written perfectly at the top of the page for a child to trace underneath, tongue between his teeth, line after line, wobbling, until his hand learned the shape. Christ wrote the pattern; we trace it.

That you might follow in his steps. Follow means follow closely, and steps are footprints: walk exactly where he walked, placing your feet in his prints, the way a child walks behind his father in deep snow. And Peter, of all people, chose the image. He had said he would follow to prison and to death, and did not, and his restoration on the beach ended with “Follow me” (John 21:19). He knows how hard tracing those letters is, and he is writing to slaves, not apostles.

In everyday life. Before you meet the hardest person of your day, picture the copybook: Christ’s letters at the top, your hand underneath. Trace one letter: a gentle answer, a silence instead of a retort. You will wobble. Trace it again tomorrow.

Why would God call anyone to suffer? Because he is making us like his Son, whose way to glory went through the cross (1:11; Hebrews 12:2). Suffering for doing good shows the world what Christ is like, refines faith (1:7), loosens our grip on this world, and prepares “an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). God is not careless of our pain; he has a purpose in it bigger than our comfort, and he calls us to nothing he has not done first. The footprints in front of you were made by bleeding feet.

verseByVerse.quote: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ suffered without sin, without lies, without retaliation or threats, because he kept handing his case to the Father, the just Judge.

He committed no sin. Verses 22–25 are one of the New Testament’s fullest meditations on Isaiah 53, applied, astonishingly, to slaves at work; this line takes up Isaiah 53:9. Peter is not repeating a doctrine he has read. He spent some three years with Jesus, saw him tired, hungry, angry and grieved, and testifies that he found no sin in him (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 John 3:5). His suffering was entirely unjust.

Neither was deceit found in his mouth. A slave suffering unjustly is tempted to retaliation and to the small deceits by which the powerless survive. Jesus did not lie his way out of a trial that would kill him.

When he was reviled, he did not revile in return. At his trial and on the cross he was mocked, spat on, blindfolded and struck, and told to prophesy who hit him (Matthew 26:67–68; 27:39–44), and he did not answer insult with insult. Peter was in the courtyard that night, near enough to see and hear (Luke 22:54–62). The Greek verbs describe something that went on and on: the abuse kept coming, and he kept silent.

When he suffered, he did not threaten. A threat is the weapon of someone who has run out of others, and Christ had not: he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). Here is perfect power under perfect control, for love. Instead he prayed, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts lack this prayer, though most modern Bibles keep it). Peter had drawn a sword in the garden; he learned from his Master’s silence what courage really was.

But continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly. The whole passage turns on this. The verb means to hand over, to deposit, and the tense means he kept doing it, through the trial and the flogging and the nails, until his last words: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Without this the passage would be cruel. He was not crushing the desire for justice but handing it on: the case was not dropped, but given to a Judge who would hear it properly. That is exactly what a slave with no court can do: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).

The Judge did not fail him. On the third day the verdict came, and the silent Lamb was “declared to be the Son of God in power” (Romans 1:4). And the one who would not defend himself now defends us: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

Why must I have the last word? Someone misrepresents you in a meeting, a relative rewrites the family history, a stranger mocks you online, and something in you will not rest until the record is set straight. We carry our reputations in public, measured and compared, so every slight feels like a threat. Beneath it lies an unexamined assumption: if I do not defend my name, no one will. Where there is no Judge above us, each of us must be his own lawyer, and a lawyer whose case is never closed cannot sleep; bitterness can keep a file open for forty years. Jesus was not passive in that courtyard; he was resting his case with someone else. Someone with his advocate can afford to let an insult go unanswered.

Does entrusting myself to God mean I must not want justice? No. Wanting justice is right, and God wants it more than you do; what Peter forbids is taking vengeance into your own hands. Entrusting places the case, with all its pain, with the Judge who sees everything and will put every wrong right, at the cross for those who repent or at the judgment for those who do not. That frees you from bitterness: you need not carry, nurse or settle the grievance. You hand it over, and when it comes back to mind, you hand it over again.

Can I still speak up or report wrongdoing? Yes. Jesus asked the officer why he struck him (John 18:23), and Paul claimed his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). Speaking the truth, reporting a crime, seeking protection or using lawful complaint procedures is not revenge. The difference is in heart and method: justice sought through proper means, without hatred, leaving the outcome with God, rather than insult for insult and harm for harm.

verseByVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ did what no follower can: he carried our sins and their penalty in his own body on the cross, so that we might be done with sin and live for righteousness. His wounds are our healing.

He himself bore our sins. Here Peter steps decisively past example: Christ does what no follower can imitate. He himself is emphatic: no one else. Bore (anēnenken), carried up, echoes Isaiah 53:4, 11–12, and is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses for carrying a sacrifice up to the altar. He carried our sins and their penalty (Hebrews 9:28). This is substitutionary atonement: our sins were laid on him, and he bore the punishment we deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6).

In his body on the tree. Not a spiritual transaction conducted elsewhere, but sins carried in a physical body, up a hill, on a particular afternoon. The tree (xylon, wood) is no poetic word for the cross: it comes from Deuteronomy 21:23, “a hanged man is cursed by God”. Peter used it preaching in Acts (5:30; 10:39), his settled way of saying that Christ went under the curse; Paul draws the same line from the same verse (Galatians 3:13).

That we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Die to sin is literally having departed from sins. United with Christ in his death, we are freed from sin’s rule (Romans 6:2–11). That does not mean ceasing to feel its pull, but that sin is no longer master: the believer can say no to it, and when he falls he no longer belongs to it (Romans 6:14). Christ did not bear sins so that we could continue in them; the atonement produces holiness rather than excusing its absence.

By his wounds you have been healed. Isaiah 53:5, and wounds is singular in Greek (mōlōps): the welt left by a lash. Some of these household slaves may well have had such marks on their own backs, and Peter tells them that the marks on his are what healed them. Healed means healed from sin, for verse 25 goes straight on to straying sheep returning. For a beaten slave the image would have gone in like a nail: he has been where you are, and his stripes did what yours never could. We will spend eternity looking at the scars by which we were healed.

If Christ bore my sins, why do I still feel guilty? Sometimes because of a sin not yet confessed; confess it, and you will be forgiven (1 John 1:9). But often the conscience is slow to believe the gospel, and keeps accusing over sins Christ has already carried. Then the answer is not penance but the cross: your sins were really borne, in his body, on the tree, and God does not punish the same sin twice. Answer the guilt with this verse, out loud if necessary: he himself bore my sins.

How can one man bear the sins of millions? Because of who he is. A mere man could at best die for his own sins; Christ is the eternal Son made man, sinless, with no debt of his own, so his one sacrifice is of infinite worth (1:19). “The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), and he bore it fully, so that God is just in forgiving everyone who trusts him (Romans 3:26). The question is not whether his death is enough, but whether you are resting on it.

Is it not unjust for God to punish an innocent man in place of the guilty? It would be, had God seized an unwilling stranger. But the one who bore our sins is God the Son himself, who came willingly: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). The Judge did not make a third party pay; he paid himself. And Christ died not as an outsider but as the head of his people, united to them as a husband to his bride, so that what was theirs became his and what is his becomes theirs. The cross is not God being cruel to the innocent; it is the holy God carrying the cost of his own mercy.

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise physical healing now? Some teach that physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement, so that believers can claim it now by faith. This commentary’s view: In context, Peter speaks of healing from sin: we were straying, now we have returned; we have died to sin. Christ’s atonement does secure the final healing of our bodies at the resurrection (Romans 8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and God may heal in answer to prayer now (James 5:14–15). But physical healing is not guaranteed in this life; believers still get sick and die, and the apostles themselves left sick friends behind (2 Timothy 4:20). The healing promised now is the healing of the soul. Christians who pray boldly for healing are right to pray; the difference is only over whether healing is promised now, and a sick believer who is not healed has not failed in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We were wandering sheep, and Christ the Shepherd has brought us back and now watches over our souls.

For you were straying like sheep. Isaiah 53:6. Sheep seldom run away on purpose. They drift, head down, one mouthful at a time, until they look up and the flock is gone.

But have now returned. The verb can be read as passive, you were turned back, which fits being caused to be born again (1:3) and called out of darkness (2:9). Sheep are not famous for finding their own way home. They were turned, by the Shepherd who goes after the lost one until he finds it, and lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:3–7): “I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed” (Ezekiel 34:16).

To the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. Two titles, both chosen with care. Shepherd (poimēn) is the tender one, carrying Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34 and John 10 with it: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11), and Peter will call him the Chief Shepherd (5:4). Overseer (episkopos) is the guardian who watches over and cares for, the same word translated bishop when it names a church officer. Peter gives the title first to Christ, and calls himself merely a fellow elder in chapter 5. Jesus is the true Overseer of his people, over all human overseers (5:2–4).

Peter had strayed. Few had more reason to write this sentence. He had strayed spectacularly and in public, and been turned back by a look across a courtyard and a charcoal fire on a beach, where he was asked three times whether he loved his Lord and told three times to feed the sheep (John 21:15–17). So the chapter that began with newborns craving milk ends with a shepherd who goes after strays: both are about being kept alive by someone else’s care.

He never loses count. We were lost, grazing our way towards the cliff edge, and the Shepherd who is also the Lamb came looking. He carried us home on his shoulders, and now he watches over our souls; he never sleeps and never loses count. We are his because he came looking.

What if I have wandered since I became a Christian? Then this verse is for you too. The Shepherd goes on watching over his sheep and brings back his own when they stray; Peter wandered after three years at Jesus’ side, and was restored. Do not stay away out of shame, as if you had to clean yourself up first: sheep are carried back, not marched. Confess where you have gone, turn back to him today, and find a faithful church where you can be shepherded. He has not stopped being the Overseer of your soul.

keyVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
keyVerse.note: Everything the chapter asks, a new identity, a holy life, patience under injustice, rests on this verse. Here Christ is no longer only the example the suffering follow; he is the substitute who did what no follower can, carrying our sins and their curse on the cross. And the healing he gives is not a reward for following well but the reason anyone can follow at all.

2.reflection:
Peter tells newborn Christians to crave God’s word the way a baby craves milk (vv. 2–3). What spoils your appetite for Scripture, and what has helped it return?

Verses 9–10 give the church titles once given to Israel: chosen, royal, holy, treasured. Which of them do you find hardest to believe about yourself, and how does Peter’s “once … but now” help?

Peter tells believers to submit to the emperor (Nero) and slaves to submit even to harsh masters, yet he himself refused when told to stop preaching (Acts 5:29). How do we tell the difference between honouring authority and obeying God rather than men? What does this passage not require of someone being abused?

Verses 22–24 show Christ as both our example and our substitute. Why does it matter that Peter puts both together, and what would go wrong if we had only one of them?

3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 completes the household instructions begun in 2:13 and widens them to the whole church, within the letter’s long section on how God’s exiles live among unbelievers (2:11–4:11).

The message. You can afford to do good to people who do you harm, because Christ has already won. The wife with a hostile husband, the husband tempted to use his strength, the slandered congregation: each is called to answer wrong as Christ did, not with fear or retaliation but with quiet goodness, blessing and a ready reason for hope. That is not weakness, for the one who walked that way first now reigns over every power that frightens them.

Why it was said. Some readers were believing wives in pagan homes; the whole church was being slandered and squeezed by its neighbours (see the introduction). Two responses came naturally, fear and the urge to answer insult with insult, and the chapter answers both.

How the chapter makes its case. Wives may win unbelieving husbands without a word, by a gentle spirit that fears nothing (vv. 1–6); husbands must know and honour their wives as fellow heirs (v. 7). The whole church is to bless instead of retaliating, trusting Psalm 34’s promise that the Lord watches the righteous (vv. 8–12). Suffering for righteousness cannot do them lasting harm, so they need not fear, but should enthrone Christ in their hearts and give a gentle reason for their hope (vv. 13–17). Then the ground of it all: Christ suffered for the unrighteous, was made alive and is enthroned over every power, and baptism marks believers as carried through judgment in him, as Noah’s eight were carried through the flood (vv. 18–22).

Where it leads. The chapter climbs from a kitchen to the throne of heaven. The silent wife and the believer who will not revile in return are copying the Lord who stood silent before his accusers. But he is no defeated martyr. He “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (v. 18), and he sits at God’s right hand with every power subjected to him (v. 22). The gentleness he asks of his people is the gentleness of people on the winning side.

For us. Ask whom you fear and whom you are tempted to repay. Set Christ apart as Lord in your heart, in the place that fear was taking, and let your life raise the question your words can then answer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Christian home is shaped by the pattern of Christ: a wife wins by goodness rather than pressure, and a husband uses his strength to honour rather than to dominate. Peter begins with the hardest case, a believing wife with an unbelieving husband. She follows her husband’s lead and lets her conduct speak (vv. 1–2), with a beauty that is inward, gentle and unafraid (vv. 3–4), like Sarah and the holy women who hoped in God (vv. 5–6). Then the husband: he must live with his wife knowingly and honour her as the more vulnerable partner and his fellow heir of grace, or his prayers will be hindered (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading This Passage Rightly

The pattern of Christ applies to wives and husbands alike. A believing wife may win an unbelieving husband by her conduct; a husband must honour his wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A woman converted without her husband was in a precarious position.

Now: This is a text about witness in marriage, never about tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Christian wife is to follow her own husband’s lead, and if he rejects the gospel, her godly life may win him where words have failed. This is Christ’s own way of answering hostility, now applied in the home.

Likewise, wives. Likewise (homoiōs), in the same way, ties this to what precedes. Peter has just described Christ, who “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” and kept entrusting himself to the just Judge (2:23). That pattern is now applied: to citizens (2:13), to slaves (2:18), to wives, and in verse 7 to husbands. Nobody in the household is exempt.

Be subject to your own husbands. Be subject (hypotassomenai) is the word for taking one’s place in an order, used of citizens and the state, and later of the whole congregation towards its elders (5:5). It describes a voluntary, respectful following of a husband’s lead (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18; Titus 2:5). It is not a claim about worth: verse 7 calls her a fellow heir. Nor is it submission to men in general: “your own husbands” (tois idiois andrasin), and no one else. On submission and leadership in every sphere of life, see on Ephesians 5:21.

If some do not obey the word. The hard case: a husband who disbelieves the gospel. A wife was expected to take her husband’s gods; Plutarch, a Greek writer of the time, advised her to shut the door to strange rites. A woman who had become a Christian alone was in a precarious position: her husband could divorce her and keep the children.

Won without a word. Won (kerdēthēsontai) is Paul’s word for winning converts (1 Corinthians 9:19–22): Peter gives a woman with little power a way that might save the man she is married to. Without a word (aneu logou) is realistic. He has probably heard the gospel, very likely from her, and rejected it; nagging, preaching at dinner and tracts on his pillow will only harden him. What is left is the silent sermon of a godly life, the one thing he cannot argue with.

Respectful and pure conduct. A life observed daily over years (2:12). A husband watching for hypocrisy finds a wife who is kinder than before, more honest, more joyful, and who does not despise him. Augustine’s mother Monica won her hot-tempered pagan husband, Patricius, to Christ in exactly this way, as her son records in his Confessions.

A copy of his silence. The Lord who won these women did not revile in return (2:23), and stood before his accusers “like a sheep that before its shearers is silent” (Isaiah 53:7). His silence was not defeat; it was the way he won his bride. A wife’s patient conduct in a hostile home is a copy of his, traced in a kitchen.

Does this apply to all Christian wives, and what does it look like? It is the pattern for all wives (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18; and see v. 5); here Peter applies it to the hard case. It looks like a wife who respects her husband in what she says to him and about him, supports his leadership rather than undermining it, and is willing to let him make the final decision when the two of them, having talked and prayed, still disagree. It does not mean she has no opinions, voice or gifts (the wife of Proverbs 31 runs a business and speaks with wisdom), or stays silent about sin. And it is never one-sided: her husband must love her as Christ loved the church, a far heavier burden. Submission is a free gift, given to the Lord, through a husband.

This is not a text about tolerating abuse. Peter describes witness within a marriage, not endurance of violence; the same paragraph warns husbands that mistreating their wives hinders their prayers (v. 7), and submission never requires a wife to endure abuse (see on v. 6). Anyone using verse 1 to keep a woman in danger is using it against its own author. Headship is never a licence to dominate but the call to lay down one’s life, as Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25); a man who uses his wife’s submission as a weapon has abandoned the very pattern that makes it possible.

I am married to an unbeliever and it has been many years. Should I give up hope? No. Peter gives this word because the wait can be long. Keep praying, loving and living the gospel in front of him. His conversion is God’s work, not your responsibility, but you may be the means God uses; many husbands have come to Christ after decades. Find support in your church; you were never meant to carry this alone. Paul asks, “how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:14, 16): there is room for hope. And your faithfulness is precious in God’s sight now, whether or not you see the outcome.

Where Christians differ: does wifely submission belong only to ancient culture? Egalitarians argue that Peter is giving missionary advice suited to a patriarchal culture, and that mutual submission without distinct roles is the Christian ideal today. Many who hold this view are faithful, Bible-believing Christians moved by real concern for women’s dignity, and they deserve to be heard as brothers and sisters. This commentary’s view: Peter’s concern is indeed partly missional, but he grounds the instruction in the holy women of the Old Testament (v. 5), and Paul grounds it in Christ and the church and in creation (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). The complementarian view holds that husband and wife are equal in worth and co-heirs of grace (v. 7), with distinct roles: the husband leads with sacrificial love, the wife follows with respect and strength. Submission never requires sin (Acts 5:29), never makes the wife inferior, and never means enduring abuse: a wife who is being abused should seek safety at once, with the church’s help. This commentary holds the complementarian view because the reasons Peter and Paul give reach back before any one culture, to creation and to Christ, while gladly admitting that godly Christians weigh those reasons differently.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman’s true beauty lies not in what she wears but in a heart at rest in God, and that is the beauty God treasures. Peter does not forbid caring how she looks; he asks what she is counting on to make her worth looking at.

Do not let your adorning be external. Adorning (kosmos) gives us cosmetic. Elaborate hairstyles woven with gold and pearls, jewellery and expensive clothes were the recognised display of a wealthy Roman woman (compare 1 Timothy 2:9). Peter tells her not to stop adorning herself, but where the adornment belongs: on the inside.

The hidden person of the heart. (ho kryptos tēs kardias anthrōpos): the inner self, who you really are when no one is looking. The pull Peter resists is not only a Roman one. Whenever we look to our appearance to be acceptable, admired or envied, the mirror has become a judge whose verdict we live for, and it always finds fault in the end. The gospel gives a verdict that does not wrinkle: accepted in Christ (Ephesians 1:6).

Imperishable beauty. That word imperishable (aphthartos) again: the inheritance (1:4), the seed (1:23), and now this. Peter keeps setting one thing beside everything that decays, and hair, gold and cloth belong to the perishing side.

A gentle and quiet spirit. The phrase needs rescuing from a caricature. Gentle (praus) is meek, strength under control, a word Greek writers could use of a tamed animal. Quiet (hēsychios) is settled, not agitated or anxious. Neither means timid, silent or without opinions. Peter describes not a personality type but a heart at rest in God: a noisy, laughing, talkative woman can have a quiet spirit, and a silent one can be seething. To a wife in a hostile household it offers composure that does not wait for things to improve, what takes the place of fear and anger once they have been handed over to God.

Very precious. The word used of the costly ointment poured on Jesus’ head (Mark 14:3). In a house where she is not valued, Peter tells her how she looks to God, whose opinion will still matter in a thousand years.

The beauty of Christ. Gentle is the word Jesus chose for himself: “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The quiet spirit Peter commends is the rest he promised, and its beauty is his likeness growing in a person, which is why God prizes it.

What it does not mean. It is not for women only: men too should be adorned with gentleness.

Is it wrong to care about how I look? No. God made beauty, and modest, unextravagant care for your appearance honours him. The danger comes when appearance becomes where you look for your worth, consumes your time, money and thoughts, or becomes a way of competing. Am I more anxious about a bad hair day than about an unkind word I spoke? The aim is not to neglect the body but to put it in its place.

How does someone become gentle and quiet in spirit? Not by suppressing your personality, but by bringing your fears and frustrations to God until they lose their grip. A quiet spirit grows from trust: the surer you are that God is in control and loves you, the less you need to fight or worry. Bring him your anxieties specifically (5:7), and learn from Christ. When agitation rises, a sharp word, a need to have the last word, take it as a signal to pray rather than to push.

In everyday life. Notice who in your church has the beauty Peter describes. Often it is an elderly woman nobody would put on a magazine cover. Tell her.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy women of old found the security to honour their husbands by hoping in God, and believing wives are Sarah’s daughters when they do good and refuse to be afraid.

The holy women who hoped in God. Sarah, Rebekah, Hannah, Ruth: they hoped in God, and that is the source of the composure. Their hope was not in their husbands or their beauty, and that gave them the security to submit.

Calling him lord. The reference is to Genesis 18:12, where Sarah, told she will have a son at ninety, laughs to herself: “After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?” Lord (kyrios), sir, was the ordinary courteous term of that world. Even in her private thoughts she spoke of him with respect.

A surprising example. That helps rather than hurts. Sarah laughed at God’s promise; she gave Hagar to Abraham and then dealt harshly with her (Genesis 16:5–6; 21:10). She spoke frankly, and once God told Abraham, “Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you” (Genesis 21:12). She was no doormat. She left Ur with a husband following a God she could not see, was twice passed off as his sister to save his skin (Genesis 12; 20), and waited twenty-five years for a son: submission to an imperfect man, trusting a perfect God, who named her among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:11). Peter holds up not a flawless woman but one whose hope was in God despite everything, precisely the encouragement a struggling wife needs.

And you are her children. As believers are Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7), a former pagan wife in Cappadocia, with no Jewish blood at all, belongs in the family of the mother of Israel.

Do not fear anything that is frightening. The surprise. Do good (agathopoiousai); frightening (ptoēsis): terror, intimidation. After a paragraph on gentleness, Peter’s picture of a godly wife ends in courage. The Greek echoes Proverbs 3:25, “Do not be afraid of sudden terror”, and wives with pagan husbands faced real threats. She is not gentle because she is afraid. A woman who has hoped in God can be quiet in a hostile house precisely because nothing in it frightens her any more, including her husband’s anger.

Children of promise. Sarah matters because of the son she bore. Isaac, whose name means he laughs, was born when it was impossible, by God’s promise alone, and through his line came the Christ. Paul reads Sarah the same way: “you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise”, children of the free woman (Galatians 4:28–31). To be Sarah’s daughter is to share her son’s kind of birth, by promise and not human strength: born again “not of perishable seed but of imperishable” (1:23). Every one of her daughters is a miracle child, born by God’s promise through the Messiah who came from her line.

Is anything too hard for the LORD? At Sarah’s tent door God asked, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14), and his angel gave the answer to a girl in Nazareth: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). He sees the wife in the hostile home and the woman waiting for decades, and the Son of his impossible promises has overcome the world, so his daughters need fear nothing.

What if my husband frightens me? Then Peter’s words are a call to trust God, not to stay in danger. If your husband threatens, hits, controls or terrifies you, that is abuse, and God hates it. Submission never requires you to endure it, and you should not keep it secret. Tell a trusted friend and your pastor or elders, and if you are in danger, contact the police or an abuse helpline the same day and get to a safe place. A godly church will protect you and call your husband to repentance. Seeking safety is not a failure of faith or of submission; it may be exactly what the courage Peter describes looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Christian husband must know his wife, honour her and use his strength for her, because she is his equal as an heir of grace, and God will not ignore how he treats her.

Likewise, husbands. The same word puts the man under the same pattern of Christ. In a world where a husband’s authority was hardly questioned, a command addressed to him is remarkable. He gets one verse to the wives’ six, but it carries great weight.

In an understanding way. Live with (synoikountes) covers the whole of married life, the sexual relationship included. In an understanding way is literally according to knowledge (kata gnōsin): he is to have studied this particular woman well enough to live with her intelligently, her needs, feelings, fears, gifts and burdens.
