That is a lifetime’s work and cannot be done at a distance, which rules out the husband who is present in the house and absent from the marriage.

Showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel. Showing honour (aponemontes timēn) is giving her what is her due. The phrase weaker vessel has been misused (see the box below), but see what Peter does with it: the weakness is the reason for honour, not for contempt or command. Because she is more vulnerable to him, he owes her more care, which turns the usual way of power upside down. He is to use his strength to protect and honour, as a man handles fine porcelain with care, not because it is worth less than an iron pot but because it is worth more.

Heirs with you of the grace of life. Fellow heirs (synklēronomois): husband and wife stand equal before God and inherit the same imperishable estate (1:4; Galatians 3:28). So verse 1 cannot mean she is worth less; distinction of roles is not distinction of worth. One day he will stand beside her before the throne, welcomed by the same grace, not by which of them was head of the house.

Prayers not hindered. Hindered: blocked, as a road is by a fallen tree. God takes her side, and will not go on hearing as usual the prayers of a man who is mistreating a fellow heir (Malachi 2:13–16). A husband cannot be a lion of prayer in the church and a bully in the kitchen.

A bruised reed he will not break. The husband’s likewise points him to the same Christ the wives were given (2:21–24), who used his strength for the weak: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (Matthew 12:20). He had all power, and spent it touching lepers, lifting a woman bent double for eighteen years, defending a weeping woman at a Pharisee’s table, and seeing his mother cared for from the cross. A husband who uses his strength to honour the more vulnerable is not soft; he is tracing his Lord’s pattern.

What does it mean for a husband to lead? To go first in love, sacrifice and service. Christ led the church by washing feet and dying (Ephesians 5:25–29). A Christian husband leads by praying with and for his wife, taking responsibility for the spiritual health of the home, listening carefully before deciding, protecting her, and putting her good before his comfort. He does not make every decision, does not demand his way, and never uses his strength to frighten her: “do not be harsh with them” (Colossians 3:19). Leadership that does not look like Christ is not biblical headship, whatever it calls itself.

How do I live with my wife in an understanding way if I do not understand her? Admit it, and ask: what she needs from you, what burdens her, what makes her feel loved and what makes her feel dismissed. Then listen without defending yourself, and pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Understanding is not a gift some men lack; it is knowledge gained by attention over years. The husband who keeps asking, listening and adjusting is obeying this verse, even if he still finds her a mystery.

In everyday life. If your prayers feel blocked, ask honestly whether there is something between you and your wife that needs putting right first. Apologise without excuses.

Uncertain wording. Peter does not explain weaker vessel (asthenesterō skeuei). A vessel is a container, used of a person made by God for his use (2 Timothy 2:21), possibly here of the body; either way “weaker” implies that the husband is a vessel too. Weaker most likely refers to physical strength, and perhaps to social vulnerability in a world where women had few rights. Not morally, intellectually or spiritually weaker: the rest of the verse rules that out by calling her a fellow heir.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church under pressure answers hostility the way Christ did: with love among its members, blessing towards its enemies and a hope it is ready to explain. Peter calls everyone to be of one mind and tender towards one another, and to repay insult with blessing (vv. 8–9), backing it with Psalm 34’s promise that the Lord sees the righteous and opposes evildoers (vv. 10–12). Suffering for doing right cannot do them lasting harm, so they need not fear (vv. 13–14). Instead they are to enthrone Christ in their hearts, give a gentle reason for their hope, and keep a clear conscience, so that the slander falls back on the slanderers (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Forgotten Half of Verse 15

Repay evil with blessing. Be ready to give a reason for your hope, and give it with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Slandered believers were told to fear the Lord, not their accusers.

Now: A life that raises questions, and answers them courteously, is the best reply to slander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole church must treat its own members with love and humility, and answer those who wrong it with blessing, because blessing is what God called them to receive and to give away.

Finally, all of you. The household instructions end and the whole congregation is addressed. Five qualities follow, all about how they treat one another, because a church under fire that turns on itself has already lost.

Have unity of mind. Not uniformity of opinion on every question, but a shared outlook on what matters most: the same Lord, gospel and hope (Philippians 2:2).

Sympathy. Literally suffering-with (Romans 12:15). In persecuted congregations that was not sentiment but survival: when one member was fined or beaten, the others felt it.

Brotherly love. Loving as family (1:22). The church is not a club of the like-minded; families are where you learn to love people you did not choose.

A tender heart. From the root the Gospels use when Jesus was moved with compassion (Matthew 9:36): felt kindness, not professional politeness.

And a humble mind. In classical Greek the root was mostly an insult, meaning abject or servile. It took the Son of God washing feet to make humility beautiful (Philippians 2:3).

Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling. Not only violence is forbidden but the returned insult, the one retaliation available to people with no power (2:23; Romans 12:17).

But on the contrary, bless. Not merely refrain. Bless (eulogountes) means speak well of, and ask God’s good on, the very people slandering you: not neutrality but active good. It is the Lord’s own command: “bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you” (Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14).

An echo of his voice. Peter had heard the Lord say it, and knew how he had prayed for the men who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Every blessing spoken over an enemy is an echo of that voice, and his church is meant to be a choir of such echoes. No one blesses a slanderer by temperament; the Spirit of the Christ who blessed his enemies lives in his people to make it possible (Galatians 5:22–23).

That you may obtain a blessing. Obtain means inherit (1:4). Not a bargain, as if we bless in order to be paid, but how life in God’s family works: people called to inherit blessing have blessing to give away.

How can I bless someone who has hurt me badly? Begin with prayer, not feeling. Ask God to do them good: repentance, salvation, what they truly need. You can pray that honestly long before you feel warmly. Then refuse to curse them in your speech: no mocking, no running them down to others. When an opportunity comes to do them a kindness, take it, if it is safe. Blessing does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, restoring trust that has not been earned, or putting yourself back in harm’s way. It means refusing to return the poison, and handing the case to God.

What about the person in church I simply do not get on with? Then the five words of verse 8 are your homework. Like-minded: focus on the gospel you share, not the preferences you do not. Sympathetic: find out what they are carrying. Brotherly: they are family by God’s choice. Tender: ask God for compassion for them. Humble: they may find you hard work too. You do not have to become best friends. You do have to love them, speak well of them, and refuse to build a faction against them.

verseByVerse.quote: For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good life is found by guarding the tongue, turning from evil and pursuing peace, because the Lord watches over the righteous and sets his face against those who do evil.

Whoever desires to love life and see good days. Peter backs verse 9 with Psalm 34:12–16, and the choice is not accidental. He has drawn on this psalm already (2:3), and it is the psalm David wrote after escaping from Achish, king of Gath (called Abimelech in its title), by pretending to be insane, scrabbling at the doors and letting spit run down his beard (1 Samuel 21:10–15). A man in real danger, with no power, getting out alive: the right psalm for these readers. Peter does not sneer at the longing for a good life, now and for ever; he tells them where it is found.

Keep his tongue from evil. The psalm’s first counsel to a man in danger matches verse 9: control what you say when they come at you.

Turn away from evil and do good. Both are needed. Only avoiding evil leaves a life empty; doing good without turning from evil is hypocrisy.

Seek peace and pursue it. Pursue is the hunting word: chase it down (Romans 12:18). Peacemakers run towards broken relationships to mend them.

The eyes of the Lord. He is watching and listening, which is exactly what a slandered congregation could not be sure of.

The face of the Lord is against those who do evil. A Christian can decline to return the insult not because it does not matter, but because God, far better placed to deal with it, has noticed it (2:23). And Peter stops before the psalm’s next line, about cutting off the memory of evildoers, perhaps leaving room for persecutors to repent.

The righteous man of Psalm 34. The psalm goes on: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken” (Psalm 34:19–20). John saw it kept at Golgotha, when the soldiers broke the legs of the two criminals but not of Jesus: “Not one of his bones will be broken” (John 19:33–36), echoing the Passover lamb and this psalm together. The righteous one on whom the Lord’s eyes rested most of all had the greatest afflictions, and his deliverance came through death to resurrection. That is the road by which the good days of verse 10 reach his people.

Does this mean that if I live well, life will go well? Generally, yes: honest, peaceable, kind people usually have better lives than liars and brawlers. But it is no guarantee of comfort in this life, as the next verses show; Christ lived perfectly and was crucified. The good days are finally those of the age to come, though many are tasted now. Live this way because it is right, because it usually goes better, and because God is watching, and leave the timing of the good days to him.

In everyday life. Pick one strained relationship and pursue peace in it this week: an apology, a message, a conversation you have been avoiding. Before you speak in a tense moment, ask: will this pursue peace?

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,
verseByVerse.commentary:
People may make believers suffer for doing good, but they cannot do them real harm, because God calls such sufferers blessed; so there is no need to fear them.

Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? Zealous (zēlōtai) is the word from which the Jewish revolutionaries called Zealots took their name; one of Peter’s fellow disciples was Simon the Zealot (Luke 6:15). Peter wants a zeal for good as hot as any revolutionary’s. The question expects the answer nobody, and verse 14 at once concedes that somebody might: two kinds of harm. Ordinarily visible good disarms hostility (2:12, 15); ultimately no one can harm the believer’s soul (Matthew 10:28; Romans 8:31).

But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake. Even if (ei kai) is put in a rare Greek form that marks something as possible but not certain. Peter is a realist; he knows what happened to his Lord. For righteousness’ sake means because of doing right, because of loyalty to Christ.

You will be blessed. Blessed (makarioi) is the Beatitude word: “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10). Peter is echoing his Lord. They can hurt you, but the worst they can do falls on someone God calls blessed for it, and cannot touch his standing with God or his future.

Have no fear of them, nor be troubled. The words come from Isaiah 8:12. Judah was terrified of the alliance of Syria and Israel, with Assyria behind them, and Isaiah was told not to fear what the people feared but to make the LORD of hosts their fear (Isaiah 8:12–13), the verse Peter turns to next. Troubled (tarachthēte) is shaken, stirred up like water. “Have no fear of them” is about the people who threaten; “nor be troubled” is about the churning inside that goes on after the threat has passed. Neither is a demand to feel nothing. Isaiah’s word to a frightened nation was not that the danger was imaginary, but that God was bigger.

Blessing in the prison cell. The one who calls his people blessed holds the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). He was persecuted for righteousness’ sake as no one ever was, and he shares his kingdom with his persecuted people, so that the prison cell, and the family table where they sit alone, become places where heaven’s blessing rests.

What kind of suffering counts as for righteousness’ sake? Suffering that comes because you belong to Christ or did what was right: losing a promotion because you would not lie, being mocked for your faith, rejected by family for following Christ. Not suffering that comes from your own foolishness, rudeness or wrongdoing (2:20; 4:15), nor the ordinary troubles that come to everyone, though God uses those too. Be careful not to call every criticism persecution. But when the suffering really is for Christ, do not be ashamed. You are in the line of the prophets, and Christ calls you blessed.

Uncertain wording. Have no fear of them is literally “do not fear their fear” (ton phobon autōn). It may mean the fear they cause, do not be afraid of them, as the ESV takes it; or, as in Isaiah 8:12 where the words come from, do not fear what they fear, do not share the panic around you. Here “they” are the persecutors, so the first is more likely, but both fit, and the cure is the same: fear the Lord instead (v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In place of fear, believers are to enthrone Christ as Lord in their hearts, and be ready to explain their hope to anyone who asks, with gentleness and respect.

In your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy. One fear drives out another. This is Isaiah 8:13, “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy”, with one deliberate change: the LORD of hosts, Yahweh, the covenant God of Israel, becomes Christ the Lord, without a word of explanation. Christ is the LORD, stated strongly and almost in passing. So the one a frightened believer honours above the magistrate is not a martyred teacher who needs defending but the LORD of hosts himself. Honour as holy (hagiasate) is set apart, revere: enthrone Christ in your heart. The heart that has Christ on its throne has no room left there for the magistrate.

Always being prepared to make a defense. Defence (apologia) is a reasoned answer, the courtroom speech, and gives us apologetics. For these readers it was sometimes a real courtroom.

A reason for the hope that is in you. Asks (aitounti) can mean demands as well as requests; reason (logos) is an account; the hope is the living hope of 1:3. They are not going out to argue; they are being asked. The hope must have been visible enough to prompt a question, and a Christian whose life raises no questions will rarely be asked. What they explain is not the atonement in general but the hope in you: why you are like this under these conditions. It is personal testimony grounded in reasons, which is why being prepared means having thought about it in advance.

Yet do it with gentleness and respect. The manner is half the verse, and usually the forgotten half. Gentleness (prautēs) is the noun of the word used of the wife in verse 4: strength under control. Respect is literally fear (phobos), most likely reverence towards God, though it certainly rules out contempt for the questioner. A harsh answer has not obeyed this verse, however correct its content: honouring Christ in the heart comes out as courtesy to the interrogator.

One question at a time. Enthroned in the hearts of his people, Christ drives out the fear of man and gives them a hope so bright that strangers stop to ask about it. And when they answer, haltingly, in kitchens and offices and prison cells, he speaks through them, so that the hope in one heart is carried to another, and his kingdom grows one question at a time.

How do I honour Christ as Lord in my heart? The heart is where fear is settled, long before anyone asks a question. To set Christ apart as Lord there is to give him, on purpose, the place the threatening person was taking. Name the fear. Whose opinion, anger or power is filling your mind today? Set Christ beside it. Tell yourself who he is: the one who suffered once for sins to bring you to God (v. 18), and who now sits at God’s right hand with every power subject to him (v. 22). Give him the decision in advance. Before the conversation, the meeting or the family visit, settle quietly that you will do what pleases him, whatever it costs. Leave your reputation with him. He has already given his verdict on you in the gospel, and no other court can overturn it. When Christ is enthroned in the heart, the mouth follows: the answer comes out unhurried, honest and kind.

What should I actually say if someone asks why I believe? Keep it simple, honest and centred on Christ: who Jesus is (God the Son who became man); what he did (lived a perfect life, died in the place of sinners, rose again); why you trust him (perhaps the evidence of the resurrection, Scripture proving true in your life, the forgiveness you have found); and your hope (you are forgiven, and death is not the end). You need not answer every objection on the spot. It is fine to say, good question; let me think about it and come back to you, and then do.

What if I am shy or afraid I will say it badly? Remember that Peter, who once could not admit to a servant girl that he knew Jesus, wrote this verse. God uses ordinary words from ordinary people. Write down in a few sentences why you are a Christian, and read it over until it is your own. Pray for opportunities and courage. And gentleness and respect, which shy people often have in abundance, are half the command: a quiet, kind, honest answer often does more than a brilliant argument.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts read “the Lord God” instead of “Christ the Lord”, as the King James Version does. The earlier and better manuscripts read “Christ the Lord”, almost certainly what Peter wrote, which sharpens his point that Christ is the LORD of Isaiah 8:13.

verseByVerse.quote: having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A clear conscience lets a believer’s life answer the slander; and if he must suffer, it is better, and within God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing wrong.

Having a good conscience. A conscience that does not accuse, because one has lived rightly: “I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day” (Acts 23:1; 1 Timothy 1:5, 19). Not sinlessness, for no wife, husband or witness obeys perfectly, but integrity: sins confessed, wrongs put right, nothing hidden, all resting on the Righteous One who obeyed perfectly in our place (v. 18). The defence of verse 15 needs a life to stand on. A man with something to hide cannot give a straight answer about his hope, because he knows the follow-up question.

When you are slandered, those who revile you may be put to shame. Again when, not if (2:12). Revile (epēreazontes) is insult, abuse; put to shame (kataischynthōsin) is exposed as wrong. It works by showing up the lie: the accusation is made publicly, the life is observed publicly, and the gap between them shames the accuser. Peter does not promise that the slander will stop, nor recommend a rebuttal.

Your good behavior in Christ. Good conduct flowing from union with Christ. What is actually attacked is not the Christians but Christ in them, which is why the conduct matters so much and why the vindication is finally his.

Better to suffer for doing good. Two things matter in this carefully worded sentence. First, it assumes suffering either way and asks only which kind: bleak and honest, for Peter never suggests that the alternative to suffering for righteousness is no suffering at all. If we must suffer, let it be for doing good (2:20; 4:15). Second, and most important: if that should be God’s will. Suffering comes only within God’s will (4:19); he is sovereign over it. Unjust suffering is not an accident, an oversight or the devil’s victory; it falls inside the will of God, which is either intolerable or the only thing that makes it bearable, and this letter has argued for the second since chapter 1.

My conscience still troubles me about past sins. Can I have a good conscience? Yes, through the blood of Christ, which will “purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14). A good conscience is not one that has never sinned, but one cleansed and kept clean by confession and repentance. If you can still put something right, a debt, an apology, a lie to correct, do it, and then rest on Christ’s forgiveness. If your conscience goes on accusing you over sins already confessed and forgiven, it is no longer telling the truth; answer it with the gospel, and if it persists, talk to a pastor.

In everyday life. Is there anything you would not want a hostile neighbour to find out? Christ’s blood is enough to cleanse it: confess it and put it right this week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers can suffer for doing good because Christ has already gone that way to victory: he suffered once for sins, was raised, and now reigns over every power. Verse 18 gives the heart of it, the righteous dying for the unrighteous to bring us to God. The middle of the passage, the spirits in prison, Noah and baptism (vv. 19–21), is among the hardest in the New Testament, but its point is plain: the risen Christ has proclaimed his triumph, and God brings his few safely through judgment, as he brought Noah’s eight through the flood. It ends with Christ enthroned and every authority made subject to him (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ’s Victory

Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Verses 19–20 are disputed, but no reading offers a second chance after death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Noah's household of eight was a small minority brought safely through.

Now: Every power believers fear has already been made subject to the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ too suffered unjustly, but his suffering was unique: once for all, the righteous in the place of the unrighteous, to bring us to God; and his death gave way to resurrection life.

For Christ also suffered once for sins. If unjust suffering can be God’s will (v. 17), here is the supreme case. But at once Peter moves beyond example. Once (hapax) is once for all (Hebrews 9:26–28), ruling out any sacrifice that must be repeated or topped up. For sins is the Greek Old Testament phrase for the sin offering.

The righteous for the unrighteous. As compact a statement of substitution as the New Testament contains. Righteous (dikaios): Christ, “the Holy and Righteous One” Peter had preached in the temple (Acts 3:14). For (hyper): on behalf of, in place of. Unrighteous (adikōn): us. One righteous man in the place of many unrighteous ones, the innocent standing where the guilty should have stood (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:6–8). This is penal substitution in a single phrase, and Barabbas, released while Jesus was led away, is its picture.

That he might bring us to God. Bring (prosagagē) is usher into the presence of, as a courtier introduces someone to the king; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of bringing a sacrifice to the altar and presenting priests for consecration. The purpose of the cross is access to God (Ephesians 2:18; 3:12): not mainly to make us safe or happy, or even to rescue us from hell, but to bring us into a presence we had no business entering. The goal is God himself. He takes us by the hand into the presence of the King and introduces us as his own: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

Put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. He truly died in his human body, and was raised to life by the Spirit (Romans 8:11), in a glorified body (1 Corinthians 15:45; 1 Timothy 3:16).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ body stayed dead while his spirit lived on; he rose bodily (Luke 24:39).

If Christ suffered once for all, why do Christians still suffer? Because his suffering for sins and our suffering for righteousness are different things. He suffered to pay for sin, and that is finished; nothing we suffer adds to it. Our sufferings are not punishment, which has been fully borne, but the path of a disciple following his Master to glory (2:21; 4:13). So your suffering can never be God’s condemnation, only his discipline, his refining, and the fellowship of the cross. You suffer as one already brought to God.

How do I come to God through Christ? By trusting him. The way in is not by improving yourself first, or by any ceremony, but by faith: admitting you are among the unrighteous, believing that the Righteous One died in your place and rose again, and coming to God on that basis alone. If you have never done that, you can do it now, in your own words, in prayer. And if you are a believer who feels far from God, the door Christ opened is still open. Come in again.

Uncertain wording. Made alive in the spirit is compressed. Some take it as Christ’s human spirit living on after death; others as the Holy Spirit by whom he was raised (Romans 8:11). The more likely reading contrasts two spheres: put to death in the realm of the flesh, our mortal life, and raised in the realm of the Spirit, the new resurrection life, in his body.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “died” instead of “suffered”. The meaning is the same, since the suffering Peter means here is Christ’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever the details mean, the point is plain: Christ has triumphed over every evil power, and God brings his few safely through judgment. The details are among the most disputed in the New Testament; Luther confessed he did not know for certain what Peter meant.

The main views. (1) Between his death and resurrection Christ offered the souls of Noah’s generation a second chance; (2) he announced his victory to the dead, without a second chance; (3) in his resurrection and ascension he proclaimed his victory to fallen angels imprisoned since Noah’s day (2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6); (4) by the Spirit he preached through Noah to people who are now spirits in prison.

The words themselves. In which (en hō): in the Spirit, or the spiritual realm, just named. Proclaimed (ekēryxen) is the herald’s word, not necessarily the gospel, for a herald may announce victory or judgment; Peter does not use the word for preaching good news here. Spirits (pneumasin), used alone in the New Testament, usually means angelic beings, not human souls (Hebrews 1:14; Matthew 8:16). In prison (en phylakē): under guard. Went (poreutheis) is the same word as in verse 22, “has gone into heaven”, suggesting one journey: the risen Christ on his way to the Father’s right hand.

When God’s patience waited in the days of Noah. Perhaps for 120 years (Genesis 6:3), while Noah built and preached, “a herald of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5). Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes, told of angels who sinned before the flood and were bound until the judgment, and Peter’s readers had very likely heard of them.

Eight persons were brought safely through water. The water that destroyed the world carried the ark to safety. Noah’s family was a tiny minority in a world against them, like the people receiving this letter, and the eight were not lost.

A herald of his own victory. While the whole world mocked, God shut eight people safely into the ark. Now the risen Christ has gone up through every realm of darkness, a herald of his own victory, and when the door is shut, every one of his own will be inside, carried through the judgment by the one who bore it for them.

In everyday life. If you feel outnumbered as a Christian, remember Noah’s eight: numbers did not decide who was safe. The ark did. Keep building, and trust the God who waits patiently and then acts.

Does this teach that Christ descended into hell, as the Apostles’ Creed says? The creed’s phrase has been read in several ways. Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) understand it of the hellish anguish Christ suffered in his soul on the cross; the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) of his continuing under the power of death until the third day. This verse is often linked to it, but on either of the stronger readings (see the box below) Peter describes neither a second chance for the dead nor a further suffering.

What about people who never heard the gospel? This verse does not teach that they will get a chance after death, and Scripture gives no such hope (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church is sent to the ends of the earth with urgency. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25); no one will be condemned except for their own sin against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12); and elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest on the kindness of the Lord who took children in his arms (Mark 10:16), and many Reformed pastors have hoped, with good reason, that all who die in infancy are his. But the right response is not speculation; it is mission. God waited patiently in Noah’s day, and he waits patiently now, while the gospel goes out (2 Peter 3:9).

Where Christians differ: did Christ offer the dead a second chance? This commentary’s view: The view that Christ offered salvation to the dead contradicts Scripture’s clear teaching that destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27), and it would be strange to offer it only to Noah’s generation. The two strongest views are the third (Christ, in his resurrection and ascension, proclaimed his triumph over the fallen angels imprisoned since Noah’s day, as 2 Peter 2:4–5 and Jude 6 describe) and the fourth (Christ by his Spirit preached through Noah to those who are now in prison). This commentary prefers the third, without dogmatism: it fits the word spirits, the link with verse 22 (angels subjected to him), the context of Christ’s victory, and Paul’s picture: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The fourth has real strength in the mention of Noah’s day, and many good Reformed interpreters have held it. Many who hold the third take the sons of God of Genesis 6:1–4 as angels who sinned, as many Jewish and early Christian readers did, pointing to the order of 2 Peter 2:4–6 and Jude 6–7; Calvin and many Reformed writers read them as the godly line of Seth, and others as kings. This commentary leaves that question open, as Genesis 6 does. Either way, the point is clear: Christ suffered and was vindicated; he triumphed over every evil power; and his people, though few and persecuted like Noah’s family, will be saved. There is no second chance after death, and no purgatory.
verseByVerse.note: One of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Main views: Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day; or after his death he proclaimed victory to fallen angels imprisoned for the sins of Noah’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baptism saves, not by the water but as the believer’s appeal to God, resting on the risen Christ, who now reigns over every power.

Baptism, which corresponds to this. Corresponds (antitypon): the flood was a picture, baptism its counterpart. In the flood judgment fell, water was its instrument, and a few were brought safely through in the ark into a new world. So the water of baptism pictures the judgment that fell on Christ, the ark of his people, and our coming safely through it in him.

Now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body. A surprising statement, and Peter at once rules out the idea that the water works by itself. It does no more for a baptised man without faith than a ritual washing does for a pagan.

An appeal to God for a good conscience. Whether this is a request or a pledge (see the box below), the saving power lies in what is happening between the person and God, not in the water. Baptism saves as the outward expression of inward faith, the believer’s commitment to God and request for cleansing, resting on Christ’s work.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The saving power is in Christ’s resurrection (1:3). Baptism saves the way a wedding ring marries you: as the sign and pledge of a union whose power lies elsewhere (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12).

At the right hand of God. Peter had watched him go from the Mount of Olives, and preached his exaltation at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The man put to death in the flesh is seated on the throne of the universe.

Angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him. Subjected (hypotagentōn) is the same word-family as the command to be subject that runs through the letter (2:13, 18; 3:1). The Christian who submits to the emperor for the Lord’s sake serves a Lord to whom every power in heaven and earth has already been made subject, good and evil alike, “far above all rule and authority and power and dominion” (Ephesians 1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). This is the letter’s answer to intimidation: every power these readers feared, the magistrate, the mob, the emperor and whatever stood behind them, is already under him. Their Lord was rejected by men (2:4), suffered unjustly (2:23), and is now seated with the authorities under his feet, and that is the sequence Peter asks them to trust for their own lives.

Why is Christ’s reign over the powers good news for me today? Because whatever presses on you, a hostile boss, a government that opposes Christians, an addiction, fear of dark spiritual forces, is already under his feet, and nothing can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39). You do not have to defeat the powers; he already has. Stand firm in him, resist the devil (5:9), and trust that he rules all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:22).

In everyday life. Remember your baptism today as a pledge you made and God sealed: I belong to the risen Christ. When temptation or fear comes, say it, and look up: there is a man on the throne of heaven.

Does “Baptism … now saves you” mean that baptism gives new birth? Some Christians read it so (see the box below). But what saves is not the water but what baptism expresses, a heart turning to God and trusting the risen Christ, which is why baptism belongs to those who can make that appeal: the conviction of the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2) that those who actually profess repentance towards God and faith in Christ are its proper subjects. Our paedobaptist brothers in the Reformed churches, who baptise the children of believers as a sign of the covenant, agree that the water does not regenerate; we differ in love on who should receive the sign, and gladly share the same Saviour.

I am a believer but have never been baptised. Should I be? Yes. Baptism is Christ’s command to every disciple (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38), the way he appointed for you to confess him publicly and be joined visibly to his people. You are not saved by it, but you are called to it, and holding back disobeys the Lord you love. If fear, embarrassment or uncertainty is stopping you, talk to your pastor. Those who truly believe but die before they can be baptised, like the thief on the cross, are not lost; but the command is for those who have the opportunity, and you do.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some others hold that baptism conveys regeneration and forgiveness, and they are taking Scripture’s strong words about baptism seriously. This commentary’s view: Peter explicitly denies that the water itself saves (“not as a removal of dirt from the body”). Baptism saves as the appeal or pledge of a good conscience, that is, as the expression of faith, through Christ’s resurrection. The sign is so closely tied to the reality it signifies that Scripture can speak of the sign as doing what the reality does, as when the Lord’s Supper is called the body of Christ. Salvation comes through faith in the risen Christ; baptism is the outward sign of that faith, rightly given to those who profess it.

Uncertain wording. Appeal (eperōtēma) is a rare word that can mean a request, a pledge, or the answer to a question. It may be the cry of someone asking God for a clean conscience, or the pledge to God that comes from a good conscience, the answer made at baptism to the question, do you believe? The word was later used in contracts for the formal question and answer that sealed an agreement, which slightly favours the pledge. Either way the verse’s meaning is not in doubt: baptism saves as faith’s response to God, not as a washing of the body.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives,<sup>2</sup>when they see your respectful and pure conduct.<sup>3</sup>Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear—<sup>4</sup>but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.<sup>5</sup>For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands,<sup>6</sup>as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.<sup>7</sup>Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.<sup>8</sup>Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind.<sup>9</sup>Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.<sup>10</sup>For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit;<sup>11</sup>let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it.<sup>12</sup>For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."<sup>13</sup>Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good?<sup>14</sup>But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,<sup>15</sup>but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,<sup>16</sup>having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame.<sup>17</sup>For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.<sup>18</sup>For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,<sup>19</sup>in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison,<sup>20</sup>because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.<sup>21</sup>Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,<sup>22</sup>who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.

keyVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
keyVerse.note: Everything Peter asks in this chapter rests on this verse. Christ’s unjust suffering is the pattern for wives, husbands and slandered believers, but before it is a pattern it is a substitution, the righteous for the unrighteous, once for all. And its goal is not merely our safety but God himself: he died to bring us to God, and he rose to take us there.

3.reflection:
Peter says an unbelieving husband may be won “without a word” by his wife’s conduct (vv. 1–2). Why can a life sometimes speak when words no longer can? Where have your words run out, and what would a silent sermon look like there?

Verses 3–6 move from “a gentle and quiet spirit” to “do not fear anything that is frightening”. How are gentleness and fearlessness connected? What do you tend to look to for your worth or your security?

Peter tells the church to bless instead of repaying evil for evil (v. 9). Think of someone who has wronged you or spoken against you. What would it mean, in practice, to bless them this week, while still being wise about safety and trust?

Verse 15 assumes that outsiders will notice our hope and ask about it. Is there anything in the way you face hardship that would make someone ask? How would you explain, in a few sentences, why Christ’s suffering and reign (vv. 18–22) give you hope?

4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 closes the section on living as exiles among unbelievers (2:11–4:11) and opens the last part of the letter, which speaks directly to the fiery trial (4:12–5:11).

The message. Christ suffered and then entered glory, and his people are on the same road. So settle it now: you are finished with the old life, whatever it costs. The end is near, so live as a church with a clear head, a praying heart, a fervent love and an open door. And when the fire comes, do not think it strange: it is a share in Christ’s sufferings, the Spirit of glory rests on you in it, and it leads to his glory.

Why it was said. These converts had walked out of the drinking parties and guild feasts that held their towns together, and their old friends were baffled, then hostile (see the introduction). Believers had died, and neighbours could say their faith had done them no good. Harder days were coming, and the natural conclusion would be that God had left them.

How the chapter makes its case. Christ’s suffering settles the believer’s break with sin (vv. 1–2). Those who slander you for leaving the old life will answer to God, and the believing dead, condemned by the world, live to God (vv. 3–6). With the end near, pray, love, welcome one another and use every gift, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ (vv. 7–11). Then the fire: rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings, for the Spirit rests on you (vv. 12–14); suffer as a Christian, never as a wrongdoer (vv. 15–16); and since God’s refining begins at his own house, entrust your souls to him while doing good (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. The chapter begins with Christ suffering in the flesh (v. 1) and ends with his dying words on his people’s lips: “into your hands” (v. 19; Luke 23:46). In between he is the Judge of the living and the dead (v. 5), the one through whom grace comes down and glory goes up (v. 11), and the Lord whose glory is about to be revealed (v. 13). The world still insults his name, and the Spirit who rested on him rests on those who bear it.

For us. Decide before the trial how you will meet it. Ask whom you need to cover in love, whose door you could open, and what gift you are sitting on. And when you suffer for Christ, do not ask whether God has left you; entrust yourself to him and do the next good thing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and the nearness of the end shapes the life that replaces it. Peter calls his readers to arm themselves with Christ’s resolve (vv. 1–2) and to treat the old life as over, even when old friends malign them for leaving it, since the Judge will set things right and the believing dead live to God (vv. 3–6). Then he sketches a church ready for the end: clear-headed for prayer, earnest in love, open-handed in hospitality, and using every gift as a steward of God’s grace, so that in everything God is glorified through Jesus Christ (vv. 7–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ chose suffering rather than sin; arm yourselves with the same resolve, and live from now on for God’s will, not for the passions of the crowd.

Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh. Therefore picks up 3:18: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous. In the flesh (sarki): in his body, to death. Peter turns back from Christ enthroned (3:22) to the road that led there, and tells his readers it is their road too.

Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking. Arm yourselves (hoplisasthe) is a soldier’s word, and what Peter hands them is not a shield but a thought. Way of thinking (ennoia) is settled resolve. Christ’s resolve was to suffer rather than sin, and to do God’s will at any cost. He set his face to go to Jerusalem; in Gethsemane he said, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42); and he went to the cross with his eyes open. He did not drift into suffering; he chose it, for us. A Christian ambushed by suffering is far more likely to collapse than one who decided in advance how he will meet it, so make the decision before the trial, not during it. And the armour is not our resolve alone: the Spirit who raised Christ supplies the strength (Romans 8:11–13).

For the will of God. Human passions (anthrōpōn epithymiais) are what everyone around you wants. The break is about direction, not perfection: we never live for God’s will flawlessly, but Christ did, all the way to the cross, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). Once you have lost something real for Christ, the appeal of what you gave up is permanently reduced: you have found out what it was worth. That is not sinlessness. It is a man who has stopped bargaining with sin.

What does arming myself look like in practice? Settle now, in a calm hour, what you will do when obedience becomes costly: that you will not lie for your employer, will not join the mockery of a colleague, will tell your family you are a Christian, would rather lose the deal than cut the corner. Think through what it might cost, and pray it through. Read the accounts of Christ’s passion until his mindset becomes familiar. Then, when the moment comes, the armour is already on.

Uncertain wording. “Whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin” is compressed, and read flatly it seems to say that suffering makes a person sinless, which is plainly untrue. It may refer to Christ himself, who suffered and is now done with sin, having dealt with it once for all (3:18). More likely, given “whoever” and verse 2, it describes the believer: whoever has embraced suffering for Christ rather than compromise has shown that sin no longer rules him (Romans 6:7). It may also allude to union with Christ’s death: having died with him, we are finished with sin as a master.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your old life has had its day; when old friends are baffled and offended that you will not rejoin it, that is no reason to go back.

The time that is past suffices. Suffices (arketos): is enough. Peter does not argue them out of their old habits; he says the account is closed. Gentiles here means pagans (2:12), as most of Peter’s readers had been, and what they want to do is the will of the culture, set against the will of God of verse 2.

Six words. Sensuality (aselgeiai): shameless excess. Passions (epithymiai): lusts. Drunkenness (oinophlygiai): literally overflowing with wine. Orgies (kōmoi): drunken night processions, often linked to Dionysus. Drinking parties (potoi). Lawless idolatry (athemitoi eidōlolatriai): abominable, forbidden idolatry. Much of it was religious: city festivals and the banquets of the trade guilds, held in temple dining rooms in honour of a patron god, ran on exactly this, and idolatry, the last item, held the rest together. Nearly every item is done in company, which is why leaving it cost these people their friends, and often their livelihoods.

They are surprised. Surprised (xenizontai) is related to xenos, stranger: the Christians have become strangers in their own town. Their neighbours are less offended on principle than bewildered that anyone would opt out, and Christians came to be seen as antisocial and disloyal to civic religion.

In the same flood of debauchery. Join (syntrechontōn): rush along with. Flood (anachysis): a torrent overflowing its channel. Debauchery (asōtia): wild living, the word Luke uses (as an adverb) of the prodigal’s reckless living (Luke 15:13). When everyone is carried along by a current, the person standing still is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him.

And they malign you. Malign (blasphēmountes): slander, perhaps as killjoys, haters of humanity or atheists; the Roman historian Tacitus could describe the Christians as hated for their abominations and convicted of hatred of the human race. The slander begins not in theological objection but in social withdrawal: you stopped coming, and they have drawn their own conclusions about why.

Ransomed from the futile ways. The break was not a matter of willpower. These readers were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from their forefathers with the precious blood of Christ (1:18–19). The current was a slavery, and someone paid to get them out. He reached into the torrent and lifted us onto the rock; now we stand still while the world rushes past, on the only ground that will not wash away. And when the neighbours malign us for it, we walk where our Lord walked: he was called a glutton and a drunkard by people who could not tell eating with sinners from sinning with them (Matthew 11:19).

Does this mean Christians should avoid social occasions with unbelievers altogether? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and we cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Peter warns against joining in the excesses. A Christian may be at the party; he should not be part of what the party becomes.

How do I handle friends who mock me for not joining in? With good humour, honesty and kindness. A cheerful “I would rather not” is often enough. Keep up the friendship in other ways: a meal, help moving house, being there when life goes wrong. Many who mock now will one day come to the one friend who did not join in. Do not be bitter if some drift away. And find Christian friends too, so that you are not standing in the current alone.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who slander you will answer to God, and believers who have died, though the world counted them losers, are alive with God. Human verdicts are not the last word; God’s verdict is.

They will give account. Give account (apodōsousin logon) is a steward’s word. Peter does not promise that they will be cleared now but that a court is coming. Christ did the same: he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (2:23). Ready (hetoimōs): the Judge is standing by, and the delay is patience, not absence. The Judge of “the living and the dead” may be Christ or the Father, and Scripture says both; Peter had told Cornelius that Christ “is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1).

Even to those who are dead. Those who are dead (nekrois) are most likely Christians who heard the gospel while alive and have since died, by martyrdom or ordinary death. That was a live pastoral problem: the taunt was that their faith had done them no good, and some in the churches may have wondered the same, as the Thessalonians had (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Peter answers that the gospel was preached to them in life for this very purpose.

Judged in the flesh, alive in the spirit. Judged in the flesh (krithōsi sarki): they suffered physical death, the common judgment on sin (Romans 5:12), or condemnation by human courts, or both. The way people are (kata anthrōpous): in human eyes. Live in the spirit (zōsi pneumati): they are alive in God’s presence, awaiting the resurrection, “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” (Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 6:9–11). The way God does (kata theon): in God’s estimation. Human verdict: condemned and dead. God’s verdict: alive. The martyrs of Bithynia and the grandmothers of our own churches are not lost; they live to God, in joy.

The shape of Christ’s own death. Verse 6 echoes 3:18. Christ, too, was judged in the flesh the way people are: condemned by a human court and executed as a criminal. And God reversed the verdict by raising him. The believers whom Bithynia buried are following their Lord down the same road and up out of it. That is why the Judge of the living and the dead is no terror to them: he has stood under the world’s sentence himself, and come out alive on the far side.

Is a God who judges not at odds with a God of love? Only if love is indifferent to evil. A God who never judged would be telling every slandered Christian, every abused child and every murdered martyr that what was done to them did not matter. Love that is not angry at what destroys the beloved is not love. God is slow to anger and ready to judge: his patience gives time to repent (2 Peter 3:9), and his judgment means no wrong is finally swept aside. And the Judge was judged for sinners at the cross, so that all who come to him find the verdict already borne (Romans 8:1).

Where are Christians who have died, and what are they doing? With Christ, consciously, in joy. To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not unconscious, nor in purgatory being purified; Christ’s blood has done that. They rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13), worship, and wait for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return, when they will come with him and we will be reunited (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17). Grieve for them, but not as those who have no hope.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a second chance after death? Some read this verse, alongside 3:19, as teaching that the gospel is preached to the dead in the afterlife, giving them an opportunity to believe. This commentary’s view: The verb is past tense (was preached), and the most natural reading is that the gospel was preached to people while they were alive, who are now dead. Scripture consistently teaches that death fixes one’s destiny (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no second chance after death. The other reading empties the urgency of the New Testament’s own preaching, and it is not needed: the natural reading is simpler and more comforting, for those who died in Christ are not lost but live with God.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the end is near, keep a clear head and a sober mind, so that you can pray. The answer to the nearness of Christ’s return is not panic or speculation but prayerful readiness.

The end of all things is at hand. The end (telos) is not merely the stopping but the goal: things will not run out; they will arrive. And the end is not a catastrophe but a Person: the one who died at the centre of history will come at its close. At hand (ēngiken): has drawn near, as in James 5:8.

Why near? Two thousand years have passed, but the New Testament never gives a date; it speaks of a nearness that makes everything urgent. The last days began at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Scripture names things that will come first, such as the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but they are no timetable, for that mystery of lawlessness is already at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7). Peter himself writes that “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2 Peter 3:8). “Near” describes the whole age: we live on the edge of eternity, and the door could open in any generation, ours included.

Therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded. You might expect a call to dramatic action: wind up your affairs, gather on a hillside. Peter says: keep your head. Self-controlled (sōphronēsate): of sound mind, the word used of the man Jesus delivered, found clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Sober-minded (nēpsate; 1:13; 5:8): alert, the opposite of the drunkenness of verse 3.

For the sake of your prayers. An agitated, frightened or intoxicated mind cannot pray. Jesus told his disciples, “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38). Peter slept instead, and was asked, “could you not watch with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40). Within hours he was denying his Lord. He has learned what a sleeping mind costs. And he had seen the alternative: that night only one mind in the garden was clear, the mind of Jesus, who prayed until he was ready for the cross and then said, “The hour has come … Rise, let us be going” (Mark 14:41–42).

Should I try to work out when the end will come? No. Concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36), and every generation that has set dates has been embarrassed. Scripture does not teach a secret rapture (the idea that believers will be taken away unseen before a final tribulation); it teaches one visible return of Christ, in glory, to raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Many dear Christians do expect such a rapture, and they share our longing for his coming; this commentary reads being caught up to meet the Lord as part of his one public return, because Paul describes it with a shout, a trumpet and the dead rising. Live every day as if he might come today, and plan as if he might not come for a hundred years.

How do I clear my head to pray? Notice what is clogging it: worry, noise, screens, resentment, too much to do. Pray where those can be shut out, even for ten minutes: before the phone is switched on, on a walk, in the car with the radio off. Write down the worries that crowd in and hand each to God. Pray Scripture, especially the Psalms. And keep short accounts with God and others, because unconfessed sin is the loudest distraction of all. A sober mind is not a blank mind; it is a mind turned towards God.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above everything else, keep loving one another fervently, covering one another’s faults, and open your homes to one another gladly.

Above all, keep loving one another earnestly. Earnestly (ektenē; 1:22): fervent love that does not slacken. Under persecution, the church must hold together.

Love covers a multitude of sins. The phrase comes from Proverbs: “Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses” (Proverbs 10:12). Covers (kalyptei) is not concealing wrongdoing, nor the covering that atones, which only Christ’s blood does. Love refuses to publish, to exaggerate, to reopen settled quarrels, to keep the account open (1 Corinthians 13:5, 7). A dozen households under persecution, meeting weekly in someone’s front room, will generate friction constantly; whether a church survives it depends on whether small offences get covered or circulated.

Without grumbling. Hospitality (philoxenoi, love of strangers) was not optional. The church met in a home, and travelling believers needed lodging, since inns were expensive and disreputable: a costly burden borne by whoever had the largest room (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). The household hosting the church is the one most likely to resent it, and resentment comes out as muttering rather than refusal. They were already opening their doors; the command is to stop complaining about the cost.

Whose sin is covered. “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1), sang David, and the Christian knows what his own covering cost: Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree (2:24). A man who has had a multitude of sins covered by that blood is the last man entitled to keep a ledger on his brother. The love that covers is the cross reproduced on a small scale: the forgiven passing on a little of what they have received in full.

The homeless Guest is the great Host. The Son of God came into his own world as a stranger, with nowhere to lay his head, lodging in borrowed rooms and eating at other men’s tables. And he has made us welcome in his Father’s house, strangers and enemies as we were, gone ahead to prepare a place for us, and set a table where the cost of the meal was his own blood, and he has never once grumbled at it. Every opened door in his church is a small sign of that hospitality.

The home as a fortress. For most of history a household was porous: servants, lodgers, relatives and travellers came and went. The modern home has become a private retreat. The historian Christopher Lasch took the title of his 1977 book on the family from a phrase that sums up that ideal, Haven in a Heartless World, and argued that the haven was more besieged than it looked. Many of us spend more on our homes than any generation before us, invite fewer people into them, and wonder why we are lonely. The house has become an extension of the self, which is why opening it feels so exposing. Peter’s word cuts across both the anxious host who wants to impress and the private one who wants to be left alone. Hospitality is not entertaining, which is about me and my home; it is making room, which is about the guest. We can do it gladly because we were once the strangers at the door, and the Host let us in.

Does love covers a multitude of sins mean we should keep quiet about serious sin, abuse or crime? No. Love overlooks many small offences and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin is to be confronted (Matthew 18:15–17; Galatians 6:1), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

How do I know whether to overlook something or raise it? A small irritation, a thoughtless word, a matter of personality? Cover it: forgive it, and do not mention it to others. A pattern harming the person or others, a serious sin, something you cannot let go? Go to the person privately and gently (Matthew 18:15). Is anyone in danger, or has a crime been committed? Then report it, at once. When in doubt, ask a wise elder.

What if hospitality is genuinely hard for me? Start small and honestly. Hospitality is not a beautiful house or elaborate food but opening your life: a cup of tea, soup and bread, Sunday lunch with whatever you were already eating. If your home is not suitable, take someone out for coffee, or help someone else host. If you are exhausted, ill or caring for someone, God knows your limits; do what you can, gladly. Peter forbids the grumbling, not the tiredness. And some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2).

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer has received a gift of God’s grace to use for others, in speaking or in serving, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.

As each has received a gift. Each (hekastos): every member has been given something. Gift (charisma) is a grace-gift, as in Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4: given, not earned, and not chosen.

Use it to serve one another. Serve (diakonountes), from which deacon comes. A gift is given for others, so no one can treat it as a measure of his own standing.

Stewards of varied grace. A steward (oikonomos) managed a household that belonged to someone else (Titus 1:7), and would be asked about it. We do not own our gifts; we manage them for God, and stewards must be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2). Varied (poikilēs) is literally many-coloured, used of embroidered cloth, and the same word as the various trials of 1:6: for every shade of trouble there is a matching shade of grace. The congregation is a fabric of many colours, and a single-coloured church has lost something God intended to be seen.

Oracles of God. Peter divides all gifts into speaking and serving. Oracles (logia) are utterances of God (Romans 3:2). Not that every Christian’s words are inspired, but that anyone teaching, preaching or exhorting in the congregation should handle it as though delivering God’s own utterances: his word, not their opinions (2 Timothy 4:2).

The strength that God supplies. Supplies (chorēgei) comes from Athens, where a wealthy citizen paid lavishly for a festival chorus, and came to mean “provide abundantly”. Practical service, cooking, visiting, giving, administering, runs on God’s strength, not our reserves, and God is a generous sponsor.

Through Jesus Christ. The gifts come from Christ: “grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4:7–8). They are shaped like Christ, who spoke only what the Father gave him to say (John 12:49) and came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). And the glory returns through him, since our spiritual sacrifices are acceptable to God only through Jesus Christ (2:5). He is the way the gifts come down and the way the praise goes up.

Glory and dominion. A man thinking rightly about gifts ends up praising God. “Him” may be God or Christ; the grammar allows either, and either way all glory is his. Dominion (kratos) is the power to rule: the scattered, powerless congregations serve the one who holds all power for ever.

In everyday life. Before you serve someone this week, pray: “Lord, supply the strength.” Afterwards, say: “To you be the glory.” And if you have been holding back, waiting to be asked or to feel ready, step forward. The servant who buried his talent thought his master hard (Matthew 25:24–25); yours is the generous God who supplies.

Does whoever speaks include prophecy and tongues today? The speaking Peter has in mind is the church’s teaching, preaching and exhortation, handled as God’s word, not new revelation. Continuationists (Christians who believe that all the gifts of the apostolic age continue today) include prophecy here, and they are brothers and sisters whose love for Christ we gladly recognise; the more likely reading is that those who speak in the church today speak as one who speaks oracles of God by faithfully passing on the words God has already given. The revelatory gifts served to lay the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon complete, Scripture is sufficient.

How do I find out what my gift is? Not mainly by taking a test, but by serving. Start meeting the needs in your church, and over time you will find what you do well, what blesses others, and what you are drawn to. Ask mature Christians what they see in you. Do not despise ordinary gifts: the person who stacks chairs, keeps accounts or visits the sick is as much a steward of God’s grace as the preacher. And your gift is not your identity; it is God’s grace, lent to you, for others.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Suffering for Christ is not strange but a share in his sufferings, and the right response is joy, integrity and trust. Peter tells his readers not to be surprised by the fiery trial but to rejoice, because it unites them with Christ and leads to his glory (vv. 12–13), and the Spirit of glory rests on those insulted for his name (v. 14). They must make sure they suffer for the name and not for wrongdoing, and then bear it without shame (vv. 15–16). Their trials are God’s refining, begun at his own house, so they entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: The name Christ gave us is worth bearing; let any suffering be for that name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the fire of persecution comes, do not treat it as strange; rejoice, because it is a share in Christ’s sufferings and leads to joy when his glory is revealed.

Beloved, do not be surprised. Surprised (xenizesthe) is the word used of the pagans in verse 4. Peter turns it round: they are astonished at you; do not you be astonished at this. The fiery trial (pyrōsis) is literally the burning, the smelting furnace. Nero would soon burn Christians in Rome as living torches (AD 64); in Asia Minor the fire was probably not yet literal, and what felt like burning was the refiner’s furnace of 1:7.

To test you. Peter says “when it comes”, not “if”. To test you (pros peirasmon) names the purpose. A trial with a purpose is a different experience from a trial without one, though the heat is identical.

Something strange. The danger is not only the suffering but the interpretation: that this is abnormal, that God has withdrawn, that other Christians must be doing it better. Peter answers that persecution is a normal feature of the Christian life. Jesus said, “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you” (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12). A hard word and a freeing one: much of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening. Timothy Keller often pointed out, in Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, that people in modern secular cultures tend to be more bewildered by suffering than earlier generations, because a view of life in which this world is all there is has no place to put it. Christians feel the pain as keenly as anyone, but they need not feel it as strange.

Insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings. The joy is not in suffering generally, but in the portion that is genuinely a share in Christ’s. Share (koinōneite) is the fellowship word: participation, not imitation (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24). Not adding to his atonement, which is complete, but sharing in the opposition the world gave him. The hostility aimed at him in Jerusalem is now aimed at his body in Bithynia, and when his people bear it, they stand with him. That is why the risen Lord said to the man persecuting his church, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

When his glory is revealed. Peter says “rejoice” twice: now, in the suffering, and then, when the glory appears, with the exuberant word: be glad (agalliōmenoi), exult (1:6, 8). Suffering, then glory (1:11; Romans 8:17). Peter had seen that glory once already, on a high mountain, when the face of his Lord shone like the sun (Matthew 17:1–2; 2 Peter 1:16–18).

How can I rejoice when I am suffering? Not by pretending it does not hurt, but by looking past the pain to what it means and where it leads: you belong to Christ so truly that the world treats you as it treated him; the Spirit rests on you (v. 14); your faith is being refined; and the coming glory is beyond all comparison (Romans 8:18). The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). You may weep and rejoice in the same hour. This joy is not a feeling you produce, but a confidence God gives as you keep your eyes on Christ.

Should I expect persecution if I live faithfully? Yes, in some form: for some believers today prison, beatings, the loss of home or life; for others mockery, exclusion, a career closed off, family rejection. “All who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). Do not seek it or provoke it by foolishness (v. 15), but do not be surprised by it, or conclude that God has abandoned you. And pray for the persecuted church, which bears the fiery trial in its full heat today.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To be insulted for belonging to Christ is to be blessed, because God’s own Spirit of glory rests on you there.

Insulted for the name. Insulted (oneidizesthe): reviled for the name of Christ, because you belong to him, not for being tactless (v. 15). Not yet imprisonment, but the daily contempt of neighbours, which is what most Christians under pressure actually face: not a courtroom but a reputation quietly destroyed.

You are blessed. The Beatitude again, as in 3:14: “Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account” (Matthew 5:11–12). Peter keeps returning to a sermon he heard on a hillside.

The Spirit of glory. The Spirit of glory and of God is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s glory with him. Rests (anapauetai) is the verb of Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the LORD rests on the shoot from the stump of Jesse, the Messiah: the Spirit who rested on the Messiah settles on an insulted congregation in Bithynia. There is very likely an echo, too, of the glory cloud that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35). The presence that filled the tent now rests on people being sworn at in the street, like Stephen, whose face shone like an angel’s as they gnashed their teeth at him, and who saw the glory of God (Acts 6:15; 7:55).

The glory cloud settled over them. The Spirit who hovered over the waters of creation, who filled the tabernacle, who rested on Jesus at the Jordan like a dove, now rests on the mocked and slandered people of Christ. The world sees only their disgrace; heaven sees the glory cloud settled over them. Glory to the Father who sends him, to the Son who poured him out, and to the Spirit who rests on the weakest saint as on a temple.

What it does not mean. Not that only persecuted believers have the Spirit; all believers have him (Romans 8:9). In persecution he is present with them in a special way.

How can I know the Spirit is resting on me when I feel nothing but humiliation? Peter does not say you will feel it; he says it is so, on God’s promise. Believers who have suffered for Christ often look back and see it: a strength they did not have, a peace that made no sense, words that came when needed (Matthew 10:19–20), a love for their enemies they could not explain. In the moment, trust the promise. The insult is real, but so is the glory, and only one of them will last.
