Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add: “on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.” The earliest manuscripts lack it, so most modern Bibles omit it.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make sure that if you suffer, it is for Christ’s name and not for wrongdoing or meddling; and when you suffer as a Christian, wear the name without shame and praise God for it.

Not as a murderer, a thief or an evildoer. The blessing of verse 14 is not for a Christian who has earned his trouble (2:20; 3:17). Evildoer (kakopoios) is the very accusation pagans were making against Christians (2:12). Do not prove them right.

Or as a meddler. It is startling to find a busybody beside murder and theft. But in a small minority already under suspicion, one who tactlessly condemns pagan customs does real damage. A Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours’ business will generate hostility and then mistake it for persecution.

As a Christian. The word appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; and here), and only here does a believer take it up as a name to be worn. Coined at Antioch, almost certainly as an outsiders’ nickname (Christ-people), it appears here to be becoming a legal charge. Half a century later the governor Pliny asked the emperor whether Christians in Bithynia were to be punished for the name itself, even without any crime, and executed those who would not deny it.

Let him not be ashamed. Ashamed (aischynesthō). There is no shame in suffering for Christ: “I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation” (Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8, 12). The name is thrown at them, and they are to catch it. No one knew better than Peter what it was to be ashamed of the name: by a courtyard fire he had said, “I do not know the man” (Matthew 26:72). Yet the one who gave us his name is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), though we had been ashamed of him.

Numbered with the transgressors. There is a deeper reason not to suffer as an evildoer: the cross. Christ was handed to Pilate with the words, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you” (John 18:30). He was crucified between two robbers, fulfilling the Scripture: “he was numbered with the transgressors” (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12). He bore the criminal’s name and death, though he committed no sin (2:22). To carry the name of the one who took the evildoer’s place, and then earn the evildoer’s sentence by our own misconduct, would make a mockery of it.

In that name. The mockers supplied the word; the Christian makes it an occasion of praise, which takes the sting out of an insult more completely than any denial could.

How do I tell the difference between being persecuted and being a nuisance? Ask honestly what your opponents object to. Your faith in Christ, your refusal to sin, your honest witness? Or your tone, your habit of correcting everyone, your neglect of your work, your political rage dressed in Christian language? Ask a wise friend, because we are poor judges of ourselves. If you have brought the trouble on yourself, apologise and change; that is humility, not compromise. If the offence is Christ himself, stand firm and rejoice.

Does this mean I should keep my faith private to avoid trouble? No. Peter tells them not to be ashamed of the name, and to be ready to give a reason for their hope (3:15). You can speak of Christ openly, kindly and without apology, while refusing to police your neighbours’ lives. The aim is that if you are opposed, it will be for the name, and for nothing else.

Uncertain wording. Meddler (allotriepiskopos) is found nowhere earlier in Greek literature, and Peter may have coined it. It joins “belonging to another” and “overseer”: one who oversees other people’s affairs. With no earlier history to go on, its exact sense is uncertain; suggestions include an informer, or someone who misappropriates what was entrusted to him. The likeliest meaning, followed by most translations, is a busybody who meddles in what is not his business.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s refining judgment has begun with his own household; if that is hard, the end of those who refuse the gospel will be far worse, so those who suffer should entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.

The household of God. Time (kairos) is the appointed season. The household of God (oikou tou theou) is the church, God’s temple and family (2:5; 1 Timothy 3:15). The idea is Ezekiel’s: when judgment fell on Jerusalem, the command to the executioners was, “begin at my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:6). And Malachi foretold that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple and sit as a refiner, purifying the sons of Levi (Malachi 3:1–5). These congregations’ suffering is not merely persecution from outside but the first movement of God’s own refining (v. 12). Their trials are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

What will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? Outcome (telos): end. The argument runs from lesser to greater, and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement. If God’s refining is this painful for his own children, how terrible will his final judgment be for those who reject the gospel (2 Thessalonians 1:8–9)? And the gospel is not only an offer but a summons: to refuse it is disobedience.

If the righteous is scarcely saved. Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31 as it stands in the Greek Old Testament. Scarcely (molis): with difficulty. Not that salvation is uncertain, or that the righteous scrape in with barely enough grace, but that they are saved through fire, through the trials this letter describes: “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). Salvation is entirely secure, because God guards us (1:5), but the road to it is hard, and Peter has never pretended otherwise.

According to God’s will. Suffering is not outside God’s control (3:17). Not one of these sufferings has slipped past him.

A faithful Creator. Entrust (paratithesthōsan) is the deposit word: hand over for safekeeping, as valuables to a trusted friend before a journey. It is the word Jesus used on the cross: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46), echoing David’s prayer: “Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God” (Psalm 31:5). Peter takes both halves of that psalm verse, the committing and the faithful God. Creator (ktistēs) is used of God nowhere else in the New Testament: a man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it, and faithful (pistos) means the deposit will be there when he asks for it. The Son committed his spirit to those hands as he died, and the Father did not fail him: on the third day the deposit was returned, glorious and alive. Into the same hands we commit our souls: the hands that formed the stars, that shaped us in the womb, that have never let one of their own fall. “I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me” (2 Timothy 1:12).

While doing good. The entrusting is done in the middle of acting, not instead of it. The hand that commits the soul to God goes on working for the neighbour.

In everyday life. Pray Jesus’ words over the thing you are most anxious about. Then do one good thing for someone else, right away, while the trouble is still unresolved. And pray for someone who does not obey the gospel; the question of verse 17 is meant to move us to plead with God, and with them.

Is God punishing me through my suffering? Not in the sense of making you pay for your sins, which Christ has fully paid: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). But God disciplines his children, out of love, to make them holy (Hebrews 12:6, 10). So ask not, “What is God making me pay for?” but, “What is my Father teaching me?” Sometimes suffering exposes a sin to turn from; often it is simply the road all his children walk. Either way, it comes from a Father’s hand, not a Judge’s sentence.

How do I actually entrust my soul to God? By handing over, in prayer, what you cannot control: your life, your future, your reputation, the outcome of the trial, the people who are hurting you. Say it plainly, as Jesus did: “into your hands”. Remind yourself who he is: your Creator, who made you and knows you, and faithful, who has never broken a promise. Then go on doing the good in front of you. When anxiety returns, entrust again. It is a lifelong habit, and the dying Christ shows its last and greatest form.

Does this verse teach that hell is real and eternal? It points to it. If even the righteous pass through refining fire, the end of those who do not obey the gospel is far worse, and Scripture describes it as conscious, eternal punishment, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46). Peter does not dwell on it, and nor should we with relish. But he does not soften it either, because only the truth about judgment makes sense of the urgency of the gospel and the wonder of grace. The fire the ungodly will face is the fire Christ endured in the place of all who trust him.

keyVerse.quote: But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the chapter, and the whole letter, its shape: suffering now, glory then, both shared with Christ. It turns the fiery trial from something strange into something familiar, the road the Lord himself walked. And it makes joy possible in the fire, not by pretending the fire is pleasant, but by knowing where the road ends.

4.reflection:
Peter tells his readers to “arm yourselves” with Christ’s way of thinking before suffering comes (v. 1). Where might obedience to Christ cost you something this year, and what would it look like to decide now how you will respond?

The old friends of verse 4 were “surprised” that the Christians no longer joined them. What do people around you find strange about following Christ? How can we stand apart without being proud, sour or withdrawn?

Verses 8–11 ask for earnest love that covers sins, hospitality without grumbling, and gifts used to serve. Which of these comes hardest to you, and why? What would one step towards it look like this week?

Peter says suffering for Christ is a share in his sufferings and a place where the Spirit of glory rests (vv. 13–14). How does that change the way you see the hard things in your own Christian life, and how can we help believers who are suffering for their faith today?

5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 completes the last part of the letter, on the fiery trial (4:12–5:11). God’s refining begins at his own household (4:17), so Peter turns to those who lead it, then to everyone in it, and closes with greetings (vv. 12–14).

The message. A suffering church needs shepherds who serve like Christ, and a whole flock that wears humility like a servant’s apron. Bow under God’s mighty hand, throw every anxiety on him, because he cares for you, and stand firm against the devil, knowing you are not alone. Suffering lasts a little while; the God of all grace will himself restore you, and his grace is the ground to stand on.

Why it was said. Persecution tests leaders first: some would serve reluctantly, some for gain, some by bullying. It tempts the flock to resent their leaders, to carry their fears alone, and to drift away from the others, where the enemy finds them most easily (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Elders are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, looking to the Chief Shepherd’s appearing (vv. 1–4). The younger are to be subject to the elders, and all are to clothe themselves with humility (v. 5), which means casting their anxieties on God (vv. 6–7). The devil prowls like a lion, so they must resist him, firm in faith, with the worldwide brotherhood (vv. 8–9). After a little while, God himself will restore them (vv. 10–11). The greetings sum up the letter as “the true grace of God” (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. Christ is the Chief Shepherd whose sheep the elders keep (v. 4), the Lord who tied on a towel and washed his disciples’ feet (v. 5), the one who went under the mighty hand to the cross and was lifted to God’s right hand (v. 6), the intercessor whose prayer kept Peter when Satan sifted him (vv. 8–9), and the one in whom God calls us to glory (v. 10). The letter ends with his first word to his frightened disciples after the resurrection: peace.

For us. Pray for your leaders, and if you lead, ask which of Peter’s three temptations is nearest. Name your anxieties to God one by one. Stay close to the flock. And whatever is broken, remember who has promised to mend it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A suffering church needs leaders who serve like Christ, and members who share his humility. Peter appeals to the elders as one of them, a witness of Christ’s sufferings and a sharer in the glory to come (v. 1). They are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, not under compulsion; eagerly, not for gain; and by example, not by domineering (vv. 2–3), looking to the Chief Shepherd’s appearing and the unfading crown (v. 4). Then the younger are to be subject to the elders, and everyone is to tie on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The flock is not theirs, and its Owner is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to elders as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to tie on the servant’s apron of humility.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter appeals to the church’s leaders not from above but from beside them, as a fellow elder who saw Christ suffer and will share his glory.

So I exhort the elders. So (oun): because judgment begins at God’s household (4:17), its leaders must be faithful. Elders (presbyterous), plural: the leaders of each local church, also called overseers and shepherds (vv. 2–4; Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). Every congregation has more than one, and a suffering flock needs faithful shepherds first.

As a fellow elder. Peter opened the letter as an apostle (1:1); here he sits beside them. Fellow elder (sympresbyteros) appears nowhere else in the New Testament or in earlier Greek, so Peter may have coined it: not authority over them but experience alongside them.

A witness. Witness (martys) is the word that would come to mean martyr, as Peter himself became. He saw Jesus’ suffering in Gethsemane and from the courtyard where he failed. His charge to shepherd the flock comes from a man who had denied he knew the Shepherd at all, and been given the sheep anyway.

A partaker in the glory. Peter puts himself and them between a suffering already seen and a glory still coming, which is where the whole letter has located its readers (4:13). He had seen glory once, on the mountain (Matthew 17:1–8), and wanted to stay; he writes as a man who knows the glory is real and that it is not yet time. The face that was spat on in the high priest’s courtyard was the face that blazed like the sun on the mountain, and both are the face of our Lord.

In everyday life. Pray today for the elders of your church, one by one, and ask God to keep them humble, faithful and unafraid.

Does Peter’s calling himself a fellow elder tell against the papacy? Here Peter, writing probably from Rome (v. 13), places himself alongside the elders, not over them (see the box below). Christians who order their churches differently, under bishops or under congregational rule, still agree that every church leader answers to the one Chief Shepherd.

Where Christians differ: was Peter the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter head of the universal church, with authority passed to the bishops of Rome as his successors, reading Matthew 16:18–19 as founding a continuing office. Many devout Catholics hold this sincerely and love Christ; this commentary differs from them here with respect, because of what the texts themselves say. This commentary’s view: Peter calls himself a fellow elder, not a supreme pontiff. Christ is the Chief Shepherd (v. 4), the cornerstone (2:6), and the head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18). Peter was a leading apostle, the one God used to open the door of the gospel to Jews at Pentecost and to Gentiles at Cornelius’ house (Acts 2; 10), but the foundation of the church is the apostles and prophets together, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and Paul could rebuke Peter publicly (Galatians 2:11–14). The New Testament knows nothing of a papacy or of Peter’s authority being passed to Roman bishops. Local churches are led by a plurality of elders, under Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders are to care for God’s people as his under-shepherds: willingly, not grudgingly; eagerly, not for money; and by example, not by bullying.

Shepherd the flock of God. Shepherd (poimanate) is the command Jesus gave Peter, “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16), and Peter passes it on. Shepherding means feeding with the word, leading, protecting from wolves, seeking the lost and binding up the injured (Ezekiel 34:1–16). Christ is the Shepherd and Overseer (2:25); these are under-shepherds of a flock God bought: Paul told the Ephesian elders “to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). Every elder handles sheep that cost the Son of God his life.

Exercising oversight. Overseeing (episkopountes) is from the word that gives us “bishop”: elders and overseers are the same office (Acts 20:17, 28). Three pairs follow, each a temptation and its remedy.

Not under compulsion, but willingly. Under compulsion (anankastōs): reluctantly, because nobody else will, in a church where being an elder made you a target. “As God would have you” (kata theon) shows where willingness comes from: not natural enthusiasm but a heart that loves God and his people.

Not for shameful gain, but eagerly. For shameful gain (aischrokerdōs; Titus 1:7). Elders could profit from the work, or the warning would be pointless. They may be paid (1 Timothy 5:17–18), but money must not be the motive. Eagerly (prothymōs) is the opposite of calculating what you can get out of the post.

Not domineering. The third temptation is power. Domineering (katakyrieuontes) is the word the Lord used: the “rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them … But it shall not be so among you” (Mark 10:42–43). Peter was there, among the ten indignant at James and John, and heard the Lord finish: “even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The model for an elder is not the Gentile ruler but the ransoming Christ. Those in your charge (tōn klērōn) are the allotted ones, entrusted to each elder, not owned by him. On leadership as service in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

But being examples. Examples (typoi) are patterns, the mark left by a seal (1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:7). Shepherds led their flocks rather than driving them (John 10:4). This is a costlier leadership: a man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying. No elder meets that standard without fault; the Chief Shepherd met it perfectly in his place, which is why a failing shepherd can confess, be forgiven and go on.

What it does not mean. “Not domineering” does not mean elders have no authority. They lead and are to be obeyed (v. 5; Hebrews 13:17), but their authority is exercised humbly, by example, for the flock’s good.

In everyday life. Whatever leadership you have, in a home, a group or a workplace, ask which of the three temptations is closest: reluctance, money or power. Then, asking the Shepherd who lives in you by his Spirit for the gladness you lack, do the opposite once. And if you are not a leader, make your elders’ work a joy (Hebrews 13:17): thank one of them this week.

What should a church member do if an elder is domineering or abusive? Speak to him first if it is safe, honestly and respectfully (Matthew 18:15). If that fails or the matter is serious, take it to the other elders, who share the oversight; this is one reason for a plurality of elders. A charge against an elder should be received on the evidence of two or three witnesses, and those who persist in sin rebuked publicly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). If there is abuse or a crime, it must be reported to the authorities. Elders are under-shepherds, not owners, and they answer to Christ and to the church.

Textual note. The KJV lacks “as God would have you”, following later manuscripts; several early ones have it, so most modern Bibles include it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful elders will be rewarded by Christ himself when he appears, with a share in his glory that will never fade.

When the chief Shepherd appears. Chief Shepherd (archipoimēn): Jesus Christ (2:25; John 10:11; Hebrews 13:20). The word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: there is one Chief Shepherd, and every elder is under him. His appearing answers the three temptations at their root. A man minding somebody else’s sheep, who is due home, will not serve grudgingly, or for money, or by domineering.

The unfading crown of glory. The crown (stephanos) is the victor’s wreath at the games, not a royal diadem: a circle of olive or pine leaves, and everyone knew how quickly it browned. Unfading (amarantinos) is from the amaranth, the ancients’ symbol of what does not wither (compare 1:4; 1 Corinthians 9:25). The crown of glory most likely means the crown that consists of glory, as the crown of life in James 1:12 is life itself: not a decoration but a share in the glory Peter has just said he partakes of. Christ wore a crown of thorns so that his servants could wear a crown of glory, and the glory is his own, shared with them.

A reward for the unseen. These elders’ work was often unpaid, unnoticed and dangerous. Their recognition will come from the only person whose opinion is final.

Is it right to serve God for a reward? Yes, if the reward is what God offers and the motive is love for him. Scripture holds out reward as an encouragement (Matthew 6:4; Hebrews 11:6), and Jesus endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). What is wrong is serving for the wrong reward: money, praise, power, the congregation’s admiration. The crown of glory is not wages that put God in our debt; it is grace crowning the work grace produced. And the faithful will cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10), because the best part of the reward is the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The younger are to accept their elders’ leadership, and everyone, leaders included, is to put on humility towards one another, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.

Likewise, you who are younger. Be subject (hypotagēte) is the word of 2:13, 18; 3:1: the posture the letter has asked of citizens, slaves and wives.

Clothe yourselves with humility. Then the scope widens: “all of you”, elders to members as much as members to elders. The verb (enkombōsasthe) means to tie on, as a servant ties on a work apron. Peter had seen it done. In the upper room the Lord rose from supper, tied a towel round himself and washed their feet, and Peter objected, loudly, and was told: “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me” (John 13:4–17). The hands that flung the stars into space washed the dust from fishermen’s feet, and then were nailed to a cross: Peter’s picture is a service he at first refused.

God opposes the proud. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, as in James 4:6. Opposes (antitassetai) is military: to draw up in battle order against. God does not merely decline to help the proud; he takes the field against them. Grace is a gift, and a gift can only be received by open hands; the proud will not hold theirs out, so they receive nothing.

What does humility actually look like? Doing the lowly job unasked and unthanked; listening more than speaking; admitting you are wrong without excuses; rejoicing when others are praised; receiving correction without sulking; thinking of yourself less, rather than thinking less of yourself. It is not putting yourself down or pretending you have no gifts. C. S. Lewis remarked that the humble man will not be thinking about humility at all, because he will not be thinking about himself. Its root is seeing yourself rightly before God: a sinner saved by grace, with nothing you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7).

In everyday life. The Lord tied on the towel and washed you first. When you are corrected this week, by a spouse, a boss, an elder or a child, try saying “thank you” before you say “but”.

I am young and disagree with my church leaders. What should I do? Respect them, pray for them, and speak to them. Submission does not mean having no opinions, or that elders are never wrong. It means approaching them with humility rather than contempt, assuming the best of their motives, asking questions before making accusations, and supporting their decisions where conscience allows. Raise a serious matter privately and respectfully, and do not stir up a faction. Age and experience may see what you do not yet see, just as you may see what they have missed.

Uncertain wording. Younger (neōteroi) may mean the younger people in the church generally, or perhaps a recognised group of younger men who served the church practically, like the young men who carried out Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:6, 10). Likewise “elders” could mean older people, but after verses 1–4 it most probably means the office-holders. The likely sense is that younger believers, who most readily chafe at leadership, are to accept the leadership of the elders.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole church is to bow under God’s hand, trust his care, resist the devil and stand firm in his grace. Humbling themselves means casting every anxiety on the God who cares for them (vv. 6–7). The devil prowls like a lion for the isolated, so they must stay alert and resist him, firm in faith and conscious of their worldwide brotherhood (vv. 8–9). Their suffering is for a little while, and God himself will restore them (vv. 10–11). Peter’s greetings sum up the letter as the true grace of God and end with peace (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bow under God’s mighty hand and trust him to lift you up in his time, and do it by throwing every anxiety on him, because he cares for you.

Under the mighty hand of God. Since God gives grace to the humble, take your place among them. Humble yourselves (tapeinōthēte) is passive in form: accept the humbling. The mighty hand of God is an exodus phrase: God brought Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Exodus 3:19; 6:1; Deuteronomy 9:26). The hand that disciplines is the hand that delivers.

At the proper time. God’s timing, not ours (en kairō). A man who insists on being lifted up now is trying to do God’s work for him.

Casting all your anxieties on him. Casting is not a separate command; in Greek it hangs on “humble yourselves”. Casting your anxieties on God is how you humble yourself. Holding on to your anxieties can be a way of insisting that the situation is yours to manage; handing them over is an act of self-lowering. Yet this is no rebuke to the anxious: the sentence ends with “he cares for you”, an open door, not a scolding. Casting (epiripsantes) is decisive: throw it (Luke 19:35). It echoes the psalm: “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you” (Psalm 55:22). “All” leaves no worry too small. Anxieties (merimna) is the word of Jesus’ “do not be anxious about your life” (Matthew 6:25–34).

Because he cares for you. The reason is not only that he is able to carry them but that he cares. The word (melei) means it matters to him, and in Greek our merimna chimes with his melei: our care, his care. Peter writes to people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, and the last word of the sentence is that they are on somebody’s mind.

Under the mighty hand, to the right hand. Christ walked this verse first. He humbled himself to the point of death, and therefore God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). In Gethsemane he did not hide his anguish; he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him (Hebrews 5:7), and then went under the mighty hand to the cross. At the proper time God lifted him, as Peter preached at Pentecost: “exalted at the right hand of God” (Acts 2:33). The road Peter commends to anxious believers runs from that garden to that throne, and they walk it in him. The hand mighty enough to part the sea is gentle enough to take our smallest care. He carried the whole weight of our sin on the cross; he will not drop the lesser burdens now.

How do I actually cast my worries on God? Specifically and repeatedly. Name each worry to him, aloud or on paper: not a vague request for peace, but this diagnosis, this debt, this child, and what you fear will happen. Then hand it over: “Father, this is yours; I cannot carry it.” Do what is yours to do, and leave the rest. When the worry comes back, and it will, cast it again, without scolding yourself. Pair it with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6–7), which reminds the heart how often he has carried you before.

Is anxiety a sin? Anxiety rooted in pride is to be cast on God, but anxiety with bodily causes is an illness: a biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up, and receiving the doctor’s help is no lack of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay alert and stand firm in faith against the devil, who hunts believers through fear and isolation, knowing that Christians everywhere are standing with you.

Be sober-minded; be watchful. Watchful (grēgorēsate), stay awake, is the word from Gethsemane: “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:37–38). Peter slept, and within hours had denied his Lord (Mark 14:66–72). He knows the cost.

Your adversary the devil. Adversary (antidikos) is a courtroom word: the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor. Devil (diabolos) means slanderer. Satan accuses believers before God (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10) and slanders them through human persecutors. He is real, personal and hostile. But our Advocate speaks for us before the Father (1 John 2:1), and his blood answers every charge.

Like a roaring lion. Prowls (peripatei): he is hunting. In Scripture the lion’s roar is the sound of a terrifying enemy (Psalm 22:13; Ezekiel 22:25), and this enemy works first on the nerves: the noise is meant to frighten before it wounds. Within a few years, under Nero, Christians in Rome were sewn into animal skins and torn by dogs.

Seeking someone to devour. Devour (katapiein): swallow up. He looks for the one that has drifted from the group, the isolated, the weak, the careless, and persecution is exactly what cuts people off.

Resist him, firm in your faith. Resist (antistēte): stand against (James 4:7), stand, not attack. Firm (stereoi): settled like a rock, the opposite of the scattering the roar is meant to produce. Resistance comes through faith, the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:16), in the Spirit’s power rather than our own.

Sifted like wheat. Peter had been hunted before, and he knew who kept him. On the night of the betrayal Jesus said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). The lion found him by a charcoal fire, and he fell; but his faith did not fail, because Christ had prayed for it. So the firmness of “firm in your faith” is not the believer’s own grip. It is the faith Christ prays for, held by the Lord who answered the devil in the wilderness with the word of God (Matthew 4:1–11) and disarmed him at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

Your brotherhood throughout the world. Brotherhood (adelphotēs), as in 2:17. Peter does not promise relief; he gives them company. Isolation is the lion’s method, and the answer is knowing you are one of many, which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to churches across five regions.

What it does not mean. Not that every difficulty is a direct satanic attack, or that we should be obsessed with the devil. He is a defeated enemy (3:22; Colossians 2:15).

Is belief in a personal devil not a relic of a superstitious age? Scripture does not picture a horned figure behind every misfortune. It speaks of him soberly: a created being, a fallen angel, powerful but limited, already defeated, working mostly through lies, accusation and fear (John 8:44). Many who have looked hard at the cruelty of the last century have found it hard to explain by human weakness alone. And denial suits him: a soldier who does not believe in the enemy will not keep watch. The devil is not to be feared as God’s equal, but taken seriously as God’s defeated rebel.

How does the devil actually attack Christians today? Mostly not with dramatic manifestations, but with the tactics Peter names: accusation, fear and isolation. He tells you that you are too sinful to forgive, makes obedience look too costly, and draws you away from Christian friends until you are alone. He also deceives, with false teaching and temptations dressed as freedom. The answer is Peter’s: stay awake, stay in the word, stay with the flock, and when he accuses, answer with the blood of Christ. He is a lion, but a lion on a chain.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your suffering is short and your glory eternal, and the God of all grace will himself mend and steady you; all dominion belongs to him.

After you have suffered a little while. The suffering is real, but it has a limit. A little while (oligon) is the phrase of 1:6, measured against the eternal glory in the next clause (2 Corinthians 4:17).

The God of all grace. Not of all power, though he is, but of all grace: goodness given freely to people who have earned the opposite, the many-coloured grace of 4:10, not rationed out but for every need. “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

To his eternal glory in Christ. Called (kalesas): God’s effectual call, which does not merely invite but brings a person to faith (1:15; 2:9). The calling looks past the suffering to its destination, his glory (Romans 8:30), and “in Christ” gives the road its shape. The prophets foretold the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1:11), and the risen Lord asked, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). Suffering, then glory, is first his story, and union with him makes it ours: we suffer a little while because he suffered once, and we will be glorified because he already is.

Restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish. Four verbs, and the emphatic word is himself (autos): God personally. Restore (katartisei) is the mending word, used of setting a bone and of mending nets (Mark 1:19), which Peter had done for a living; it assumes damage. Confirm (stērixei), set fast, is the word the Lord used to Peter: “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32), and here Peter does just that. Strengthen (sthenōsei): make strong. Establish (themeliōsei): lay on a foundation. Those God truly calls he keeps to the end (Philippians 1:6). He mends what is broken, steadies what is shaking, strengthens what is weak, and sets on rock what was sinking, and he does it himself; Peter had been broken and mended.

To him be the dominion. Peter has just named the prowling lion; he ends by saying whose the dominion actually is. The devil roars, but God rules.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that suffering will end in this life. Restoration may be partial now and complete in glory. But it is certain.

In everyday life. Pray this promise back to God, naming the broken thing. Then look for one person in your church who is broken by suffering, and be one of the hands God uses to strengthen them, as Peter was told to strengthen his brothers.

What if I feel broken beyond repair? Then this verse was written for you. Restore assumes real damage, and Peter does not say the breaking did not matter; he says God himself will mend it. That mending may begin now, slowly, through his word, his people, prayer and time, and sometimes through a biblical counsellor and the doctors he provides; and it will be complete when Christ appears. Peter had been broken by his own denial, and Christ restored him on a beach. The God of all grace has never yet met a soul too broken for him.

Textual note. The KJV reads “glory and dominion”, following later manuscripts that add glory; the earliest have dominion alone.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter sums up everything he has written as the true grace of God, urges his readers to stand in it, and sends greetings and peace from the church in Rome.

By Silvanus. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion who sang hymns at midnight in the jail at Philippi (Acts 16:25), now carrying Peter’s letter. By (dia), through: he probably helped with the writing, carried the letter, or both (see the introduction).

I have written briefly. Five chapters, and a lifetime of experience compressed into them (compare Hebrews 13:22).

The true grace of God. After five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, Peter calls the whole thing grace: not advice, not endurance training, but true grace (alēthē charin). And the grace has a name. The prophets, Peter wrote, spoke of the grace that was to be yours as they searched out the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1:10–11). The true grace of God is Christ himself, crucified and glorified, given to exiles.

Stand firm in it. Not produce it, or earn it: stand in it, as a man stands on solid ground in an earthquake.

She who is at Babylon. “She” is almost certainly the church there (compare 2 John 1), and Babylon very probably Rome (see the introduction and the box below). Calling the capital Babylon reminds them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in exile as the church in Bithynia. And likewise chosen (syneklektē), chosen together with you, hands them back the word he opened with: “elect” (1:1).

And so does Mark, my son. John Mark, who abandoned Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13), and was later restored, so that Paul could call him “very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). “My son” is affection, not kinship. Peter had gone to Mark’s mother’s house in Jerusalem when the angel freed him from prison, and found the church praying there (Acts 12:12). Early tradition, from Papias, says that Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down what Peter preached in his Gospel. Two men who had both failed and both been restored, standing together at the end.

The kiss of love. A family greeting, used in the early church (Romans 16:16): slave and master, Jew and Gentile, greeting each other as brother and sister. The letter that has spoken so much of hostility ends with an instruction to touch each other.

Peace to all of you who are in Christ. Peace (eirēnē, the Hebrew shalom, wholeness), offered to people who had little of it, by a man soon to die in the city he calls Babylon. It was the first word the risen Lord spoke to the disciples in the locked room: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). Peter ends where his Lord began.

Grace that holds in Babylon. This is the true grace of God: that the Father chose exiles, the Spirit set them apart, the Son ransomed them with his blood; that he caused them to be born again to a living hope, guarded them by his power, refined them in the fire, and called them to his eternal glory. It is grace that holds in Babylon and Bithynia, that turned a denier into an apostle and a deserter into an evangelist. And over every scattered, slandered, suffering child of God, the last word is his: peace, in Christ.

In everyday life. Read 1 Peter through in one sitting this week; it takes about twenty minutes. Then write one sentence on what the true grace of God means for your life right now.

What does it mean to stand firm in grace? Refusing to move off the ground God has put you on: not sliding into earning your standing, as though suffering meant you had not done enough; into despair, as though grace had failed; or into compromise, as though grace could be kept while denying Christ. You are chosen, born again, ransomed, guarded, loved, called to glory: keep coming back to it in the word, at the Lord’s Table, among his people. Grace is not only how you began; it is where you stand every day until he comes.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? What is commanded is warm, holy affection, in the form one’s culture uses for it.

Uncertain wording. “She who is at Babylon” is not explained. “She” is most likely the church, since “church” is feminine in Greek and “likewise chosen” fits a congregation, though some have suggested Peter’s wife, who travelled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5). Babylon is most likely a name for Rome, as in Revelation (14:8; 17:5; 18:2); the old Babylon in Mesopotamia was largely deserted, and a Roman fort in Egypt called Babylon is a less likely suggestion.

Textual note. The KJV reads “wherein ye stand”, a statement rather than a command, following later manuscripts; the earliest have the command.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.

keyVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you.
keyVerse.note: Peter gathers the whole letter into one promise. The suffering is real but short, the glory is eternal, and the road between them runs through Christ. The four verbs assume real damage, and the emphatic word is “himself”: the God of all grace does not delegate the mending of his people.

5.reflection:
Peter names three temptations of leadership: serving under compulsion, for gain, or by domineering (vv. 2–3). How do these show up in church life, at home or at work? How can we pray for and encourage those who lead us?

Peter tells everyone to “clothe yourselves” with humility, remembering the Lord who tied on a towel and washed his disciples’ feet (v. 5). What does humility look like in practice in our church, and where do you find it hardest?

In verses 6–7, casting our anxieties on God is how we humble ourselves. What worries are you holding on to as if they were yours to manage? What would it look like to hand them over, specifically, this week?

The devil hunts the isolated, and Peter answers with “your brotherhood throughout the world” (vv. 8–9). Who in our fellowship might be drifting away or standing alone, and how can we draw them back in?
